#788. MC Lyte ‘Tickled Pink’ by Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction

She joins Queen Latifah, Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti & Gram Parsons as early influence honorees.

Lana Moorer — aka MC Lyte — first made history in 1988 as the first female rapper to release a full-length solo album: Lyte as a Rock. Now her pioneering achievements will take center stage tomorrow (Nov. 14) when she’s inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame with the early influence award. Also being inducted alongside her are fellow 2026 early influence honorees Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti, Gram Parsons and sister in rap Queen Latifah. Related Aria Vega Wins Best New Artist at the 2026 Latin Grammys: 'Dreams Know No Fear' On Winning First Latin Grammy, Camila Fernández Thanks Expectant Baby for 'Strength to be Here' 50 Cent Trolls Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Affair With 'P.I.M.P.' Music Video AI Deepfake: 'Jensen Don't Sweat It' Explore MC Lyte Queen Latifah Salt-N-Pepa See latest videos, charts and news

Chatting with Billboard ahead of the ceremony, Lyte says she and Queen Latifah “are going to have fun. La and I recently had a chance to talk, and we’re just amazed by these milestones in our lives. She was there to introduce me for the first hip-hop performance at the White House for the Obamas [2014]. I was there to help produce her tribute segment at the Kennedy Center Honors [2023]. Now here we are together being awarded as early influencers by one of the most prestigious organizations in the music industry. We’re tickled pink.”

Other milestones in MC Lyte’s storied career include being the first solo female rapper to earn a gold record (for her 1993 top 10 hit “RuffNeck”); first solo female rapper nominated for a Grammy; first rapper to perform at Carnegie Hall and the first solo female rapper to gain entry on the Billboard 200 (with 1989 sophomore set Eyes on This). Along the way, the Brooklyn-raised rapper-songwriter scored additional hits such as “Poor Georgie,” “Keep On, Keepin’ On” (with Xscape) and “Cold Rock a Party.”

Born out of her poetry writing, Lyte’s smooth conversational style — paired with her distinctive, bass-punched voice — made people sit up and take notice of the small dynamo, who could also hold her own as a battle-ready emcee. Equally arresting were her sharp, incisive lyrics as she helped bring social consciousness to the hip-hop forefront, addressing such topics as cocaine addiction in her debut single “I Cram to Understand U (Sam).” The early activist also joined KRS-One’s Stop the Violence Movement and appeared on the initiative’s chart-topping benefit single “Self-Destruction.” Lyte has since supported women’s rights, voter education and other causes, in addition co-founding the Hip-Hop Sisters Network in 2006.

Not one to rest on her laurels, MC Lyte operates the production, artist development and management company Sunni Gyrl Inc. and has also branched into film and television via 3L Productions. She teamed with Grammy-winning songwriter/producer Warryn Campbell for her first studio album in nine years, 1 of 1. The 2024 release features guest appearances from Stevie Wonder, Common, Queen Latifah, Q-Tip and Big Daddy Kane, among others.

Below, MC Lyte looks back with Billboard at the road she traveled to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

What moment made you declare, “Rap is what I’m going to do”?

There were two phases. First, when I said I wanted to be onstage at the theater with my mom watching Dreamgirls. But when I wanted to actually rap, it was because of hearing Salt-N-Pepa. Anybody who has ever heard the story of my life knows that’s when I believed I could do it.

I was in the third-floor window of Hammel Projects in Far Rockaway, Queens at my grandfather’s house. There was a group of guys with a huge boombox downstairs, and I heard this man’s voice coming from the speaker. It was melodic but strong and deep. That’s what brought me downstairs. It was Rakim with “Eric B. Is President.”

Once I got all the way downstairs, I heard some women rapping, It was Salt-N-Pepa doing “The Showstopper.” That’s when I said, “Oh my God, I’ve got to do this!” In school, I wrote poetry and rhymes, but it was just to pass the time after we ate lunch. Up until then, I had heard Sha-Rock from the Funky Four 4+1 and Roxanne Shanté. But it had never dawned on me that I could actually do it for real.

Who were some of your other early influencers as you began this trajectory?

Definitely The Sequence with Angie B. [neé Stone], Blondy and Cheryl the Pearl. I knew all of the words and all of the sassiness they put into “Funk You Up” with the [refrain] “Ring-ding-dong /Ring a ding-ding-ding-dong.” There was Melle Mel {Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five] with his storytelling in “The Message” and “White Lines (Don’t Do It).” I wanted to create my own songs that would be able to help my generation keep away from drugs. And Slick Rick and Doug E. Fresh’s “La Di Da Di”: Once again, I was enveloped in these stories.

Plus coming from a household where my mom listened to a lot of folk songs and artists like James Taylor and Carole King: people who also told stories. So I had many influencers in KRS-One, Spoonie G and Just-Ice, as well as OG’s like Rick James and Teena Marie.

What’s been the easiest part in arriving at this career pinnacle — and the hardest?

The easiest was submitting to who it is that I am naturally. There was never a gimmick about me or my brand. I never felt like I had to switch gears because of gimmicks getting old. I just was me. The girl down the block, your home girl, somebody in school, somebody you know. I just fit into what felt like somebody in the neighborhood.

The hardest part was just the business. When you come in as young as I was — which so many of us did — we didn’t really understand the business side of what makes this all work. You can either get into the groove of what it really is — a business – or you can fight and wind up hurting along the way. I still don’t know an artist that enjoys looking at spreadsheets. That’s not what we want to spend our time doing. We want to create. But the truth is, if you’re ever going to really understand how it works, then you’ve got to be okay with putting on that other hat.

In building your legacy, you’ve expanded into various creative arenas beyond music. What projects are in the wings?

Our company is co-executive-producing a new sitcom. I’m acting and directing in it. And we’ve got a slate of movies going into production in 2027. There’s also a new YouTube series I filmed in Charlotte, North Carolina with VanVan that I’m excited about. On the music side, we’re developing some new artists. And I recently performed sold-out shows at City Winery Atlanta and City Winery Nashville [part of her national Road to the Hall of Fame tour].

Because it keeps me in touch with people who love the music that I’ve done over the years. It feels as though we’ve grown up together. And honestly, we have. It’s been 40 years of music from me and from [labels] First Priority, Atlantic and EastWest. Being with a major, an indie and then with Warryn Campbell; they’ve gone through the journey with me. Not only do I owe it to them, I owe it to myself to stay connected to what has nourished me in my career. And it feels good. Once I get in those rooms, it feels like I’m home. And I believe they feel the same way because they keep coming back.

Lastly, what do you want your legacy to be?

I just want to be known as someone who wasn’t afraid to dream and then actively reach for my goals while inspiring others to do the same in their lives.

#787. Julianne Hough Reacts to Derek Hough’s Sister-to-Lover Moment on DWTS

After Derek Hough reacted to fellow Dancing With the Stars judge Carrie Ann Inaba’s viral sister-to-lover comment on the show, his sister Julianne Hough shared her response.

An awkward moment on Dancing With the Stars basically left Julianne Hough thinking, “Oh, brother.”

The DWTS co-host reacted to a cringey moment from the Nov. 10 episode when her brother—and judge on the competition series—Derek Hough made a quip about sibling dynamics.

ICYMI, after Paralympian Ezra Frech and his pro partner Daniella Karagach, who have detailed their sibling-like relationship this season, performed a sensual Argentine tango, they received some shocking praise from judge Carrie Ann Inaba.

“You were able to stay so centered on yourself while also delivering the story that I want so much with this dance,” she said. “The intimacy, turning your sister into your lover for one night is all good.”

As Ezra and Daniella were left in surprise, co-host Alfonso Ribeiro said, “Sister lover, that’s awkward.” And as the mic was turned over to Derek, he quipped with laughter, “Tell me about it. That was weird.”

The moment prompted a flurry of comments online, as fans pointed out how Julianne and Derek have been paired up for some sensual dances over the years. As one fan wrote on Threads, “Derek adding in ‘tell me about it’ after Carrie Ann gave Ezra and Daniella credit for doing an intimate dance when they feel like siblings had me GIGGGGGGGLING.”

After all, the 38-year-old only added a shrugging emoji while sharing a Thread post to her Instagram Stories Nov. 12 that read, “Derek adding in ‘tell me about it’ after Carrie Ann gave Ezra and Daniella credit for doing an intimate dance when they feel like siblings had me GIGGGGGGGLING.”

But Julianne appeared to sidestep the awkwardness with one smooth move. After all, the 38-year-old re-posted the comment on her Instagram Story and simply added a shrugging emoji to prove her nonchalance.

But while Julianne may have shimmied away from this week’s snafu, it’s not the first sibling-centric shuffle that Carrie Ann has caused between her and Derek. In fact, after Carrie Ann paired them up in 2014 for an intimate routine, fans thought the Houghs were married.

“Our first thing that we ever did on Dancing with the Stars was the live tour,” Julianne said on a September 2025 episode of the Chicks in the Office podcast. “Carrie Ann was the one who choreographed everything, and she got us to do a rumba together. You guys, that’s the dance of love that my brother and I had to dance together.”

“Our names in the program were ‘Derek and Julianne Hough,’ so everybody thought we were married and were doing this rumba,” Julianne continued. “When people found out we were brother and sister? I remember there was one venue, and we just heard, ‘That’s just wrong!’”

For a deeper dive into the siblings’—yes, siblings’—family tree, keep reading…

The Hough family patriarch is originally from Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, and met future wife Mariann Heaton on the ballroom team at Ricks College (now Brigham Young University-Idaho).

Bruce and Mariann—both from Mormon families and the children of ballroom-dancing parents—settled in Salt Lake City. There he worked as a communications executive and co-founded supplement maker Nutraceutical Corporation, which, according to Deseret News, reached a valuation of $300 million under his watch before it was sold in 2017.

Bruce also ventured into politics, serving two terms as state Republican Party chair and running for congress in 2023.

While he didn't win that race, he told Deseret News at the time that he was running for his family's future. "I’ve got 10 kids, I’ve got 22 grandkids and growing," he explained. "And I really feel that America’s promise is in jeopardy for those grandkids especially."

Of his most famous offspring, he quipped, "I never thought that those dance lessons would pay off,” noting that he took the most pride in hearing from others that son Derek Hough and daughter Julianne Hough were some of the "kindest people…in the entertainment business.”

In addition to Derek and Julianne, Bruce shares daughters Sharee Hough Selman, Marabeth Poole and Katherine Hough with Mariann. After they divorced in the late 1990s, he married Debra Francom Hough, also a parent of five.

Mariann grew up in Idaho Falls with three brothers.

She and Bruce were in the process of divorcing when Julianne and Derek, then 10 and 13, moved to London to attend the Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts.

Their leaving was "devastating," Mariann recalled on a 2019 episode of The Minds Gym podcast. But they wanted to dance and, she explained, "The biggest thing that kept me going is that I grew up feeling very dominated over and controlled. Love my parents, but that was like a generational thing."

However, she added, "I'm grateful for that now because…it made me sway to I love having free agency." It was also "so important" for her to pass that on to her kids, she said, and "all of them are so not afraid to go travel and do all these things."

Mariann, now based in Franklin, Tenn., is a painter and has credited husband Aaron Nelson for supporting and encouraging her work as an artist.

Sharee married husband Mark Selman when she was 19 and they share six kids.

The eldest of Bruce and Mariann's brood danced at Ballet West in Utah and these days runs her own fitness business, Hough Werks, teaching yoga and dance.

Her "dynamic" firstborn "just came into this world with a lot of energy," Mariann said on The Minds Gym. Sharee's "little mind was just going all the time, just super creative" and "self-motivated."

Moreover, with 11 years between Sharee and her youngest sister, "Julianne thinks she has two moms."

Marabeth is "just a beautiful spirit" who "loves her own space," Mariann said of her second child, and she "puts on these little retreats in Nashville for women."

She left Utah for Music City to "be a country star," baby sister Julianne shared on the Not Skinny but Not Fat podcast in September 2025, and now makes the most of her positive energy as a realtor and holistic health coach, as well as a singer-songwriter.

Marabeth married Michael Poole in 2002 and they live in Nashville with son Aidan.

Daughter Katherine, a mother of three, "just makes you smile," Mariann said on The Minds Gym, "and she's just real."

The esthetician was in a relationship with Tony Schnur before his death from brain cancer in 2023. "It’s unfair that I found my soulmate, my best friend, my partner in life, only to lose you too soon," Katherine posted on Instragram in February 2025, marking the second anniversary of his passing. "I miss you every day."

But Katherine has persevered, Julianne gushing on Not Skinny But Not Fat, "She has three beautiful daughters and she has all these activities and she plans all these things, and I'm in awe of her."

And on Sept. 24, 2025, Katherine shared that she had found love again, writing on Instagram alongside a montage of sweet photos, "After walking through so much loss and heartache, I never imagined I’d find this kind of love again. Chris is the man I prayed for, kind, generous, loving, patient, and such a gift not only to me but to my girls."

Born May 17, 1985, Derek joined Dancing With the Stars as a pro in 2007. He won the Mirrorball Trophy a record six times and is a four-time Emmy winner for choreography.

After his last competitive turn around the floor in 2016, Derek returned to DWTS as a fulltime judge in 2020.

He met fellow dancer Hayley Erbert in 2015 and, after navigating some "insane obstacles," as he put it on Couple Things With Shawn Johnson and Andrew East, they got married in August 2023.

As a couple they powered through Hayley's life-threatening health scare, a brain hemorrhage that required emergency surgery just four months after their wedding, and in July 2025 they announced they were expecting their first child together.

Posting a photo of dad Bruce dancing at his and Hayley's wedding, Derek wrote on Facebook in April 2024, "Smart, kind and thoughtful. I hope to be as good as a father as he has been to his family."

The baby of the Hough family was born July 20,1988. She joined DWTS in 2007 along with Derek and proceeded to win her first two seasons on the show.

She left in 2009 to pursue acting and scored a breakthrough role in 2010's Burlesque (though her big-screen debut was actually playing an unnamed Hogwarts student in 2001's Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone) before scoring the lead in the 2011 Footloose remake. Julianne returned to the ballroom as a judge from 2014 to 2017, winning an Emmy for choreography along the way, and has cohosted DWTS with Alfonso Ribeiro since 2023.

Julianne married Brooks Laich in 2017 but they split up in 2020, eventually finalizing their divorce in 2022.

She said on The Jamie Kern Lima Show in 2024 that going through a divorce gave her a chance to "reconnect" with her mom and dad, and they "showed up" for her.

"I needed that," Julianne explained. "I reclaimed my parental relationship with them and I got to be the kid and they got to take care of me. And that was the most healing [thing]."

Reflecting on her and Derek becoming the stars of the family, Julianne said on Not Skinny But Not Fat that there was "no jealousy" between their other siblings, "but there is a sadness that maybe there wasn't an opportunity for them to experience it."

Sharee, Marabeth and Katherine are "so, so, so happy," Julianne continued. "They have great lives, and they love their life. But we had an opportunity that they didn't have, and it's hard.”

And while she and Derek have a special connection, "they were super close as sisters growing up,” Julianne said. “So, I didn't get to have the closeness of sisters and that bond. [And] they have marriages and kids and I don't have that experience."

Meanwhile, all five siblings "get along really well," Mariann said on The Minds Gym. "I think the hard part is being away from each other, because there is some kind of a synergy when they all get together."

#786. How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd

Maurucio Pochettino (right) was first mentioned as a contender to manage Manchester United when Louis van Gaal was sacked in May 2016

When Mauricio Pochettino was asked the three Premier League managers he would have loved to have played for, he was unequivocal.

"Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson," replied Pochettino, who on Friday was named Manchester United manager.

In 2023, the Argentine - then at Chelsea, and dressed in full Blues training gear - was being interviewed by Sky Sports. Still he felt a need to express his adoration for Ferguson.

Six years prior to that interview, while managing Tottenham, he had shared lunch with the legendary former United manager.

"When I was young, when I started my career as a manager, he was always my inspiration, my reference," Pochettino said.

"And when you can share two hours with a person who was the greatest manager in the history of football, you can only enjoy."

Hiring United managers has been complicated since Ferguson's departure in 2013, and one of the most prominent complications has been a back-and-forth around the club's DNA.

For some, winning by any means necessary should take precedence, while others believe the style of play and cultural heritage of United's most successful period is vital to the club's identity.

In recent years, United's managerial merry-go-round has alternated between European coaches with their own fixed styles of play, and former players from the Ferguson era.

But between his tactics of choice and his adoration for the former United boss, Pochettino may be uniquely placed to bridge the gap between both camps.

Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better

Michael Carrick's United produced a series of good results to finish last season with a run unmatched by any other team in the league. They looked great, but it was a greatness built on attacking in a transition-heavy manner.

Under Carrick, in games they had less than 50% of the ball, they only lost once. In those 13 games, they boasted a win-rate of 62%. This dropped to 36% in games they had the majority of possession.

This style of play suited their direct attackers and protected their defenders.

At the same time, Casemiro's set-piece prowess provided United a reliable way to break the deadlock against deep defences - something they have struggled with this season.

With United a goal up, opponents stepped forward, giving Carrick's men more space. They could play to their strengths again, attacking quickly. It worked.

But teams at the top are reluctant to play in this way. Carrick's vision for United was a side that played slick football, with short passes in build-up intuitively, referencing Paris St-Germain's midfield three as a source of inspiration.

Building up in this manner, to entice and escape from pressure, before looking to find the forwards quickly, was the plan Carrick was working towards.

This didn't come to fruition and trying to take United from a successful counter-attacking side to one that could reliably beat teams while keeping the ball was the same hurdle that undid Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Erik ten Hag.

Former players under Sir Alex Ferguson, both Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Michael Carrick leaned into Unitedâs historic style when crafting their game-models

Pochettino gives United an interesting solution to this problem.

In his own words, he has described his sides as needing "to be protagonists, always press high, work hard and be dynamic". He refers to himself as a "disciple" of the legendary Argentina boss Marcelo Bielsa, who he played for.

If you wanted an immediate comparison in the Premier League to a coach who resembles Pochettino's ideas in possession, it would be worth looking at Liverpool's Andoni Iraola, who similarly cites Bielsa as his reference.

These are coaches who, while taking the initiative, encourage vertical football. For as different as the clubs are, both the fans of United and Liverpool have enjoyed success when their teams have played high-octane football.

This summer's World Cup was a strong showcase of Pochettino's style of play and his recent tactical adaptation.

Rather than a fixed, positional style of play - akin to the work of somebody like Manchester City's Enzo Maresca - Pochettino's USA had only certain players being tasked with holding their position.

This approach posed problems for teams who defended in a zonal manner - defending specific areas rather than individual players.

The US midfielders being able to move freely meant they could step into areas of the pitch between the zones that were being defended, which resulted in their players often being unmarked with time and space on the ball.

By playing in close proximity to each other in the middle of the pitch, the US found another benefit.

Small-space passing combinations helped draw the opposing team up towards the ball and combined with clever off-ball movement to stretch the pitch, allowed the US to find their striker with few defenders around him.

Pochettino's men looked to thread through-balls in behind and early after enticing the opposition's press and the speedy Folarin Balogun was able to turn those chances into goals.

Here is a good example of USA's fluid midfield four under Pochettino. The right-sided midfielder McKennie has placed himself near his three midfield team-mates, leaving the right half-space empty. With a four against three in that area of the pitch, USA are best placed to play quick combinations before looking to find their attackers in space.

Here we can the swapping of left-winger Pulisic and left-back Robinson. In this example, Robinson inverts into the fluid midfield four with Pulisic positioned on the touchline for balance. When out wide, Pulisic was able to showcase impressive one-against-one dribbling throughout the match too.

This combination of a fluid midfield, small-space passing and direct through-balls doesn't sound dissimilar to what Carrick was trying to move towards implementing this season.

And although that may worry United fans, the similarity in principles will benefit the players.

"My philosophy is to give a freer style with a good organisation," were Pochettino's words in 2014.

Although philosophically similar, that latter part - a clearer organisation to his freer style - is likely to be what Carrick was unable to reliably offer his players.

For fans of top sides, fast-paced, vertical football tends to be accepted when it comes from a place of being proactive - think Ferguson's United or Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool - wanting to keep the ball, but not passing it for passing's sake.

Fast-paced, vertical football tends to be frowned upon when it comes from a place of conceding possession and defending your own goal for long periods of the match.

The first half of Carrick's stint did appear proactive, while his 4-2-4 press worked well. Leaving four players high was a risk that allowed them to win the ball back and score quickly, but as teams figured this out, United failed to adapt.

There also appeared to be a drop in the team's fitness the longer United went from the departure of ex-boss Ruben Amorim, who left United well conditioned, albeit on the back of a schedule without European football.

Here we see United's narrow 4-2-4 defensive shape in the first half against Como

Hiring Pochettino will immediately begin the process of turning United into a well-drilled side, capable of applying intense pressure, likely in a co-ordinated manner.

Pochettino enjoyed relative success with Spurs, built on this intensity and co-ordination, that differentiated him from the rest of the league.

With that unique selling point more common now than a decade ago, how he builds on it will dictate how his tenure unfolds.

But watching Brighton this season, he can be assured that an approach founded on intensity off the ball can work in the Premier League in 2026, with Fabian Hurzeler's men second in the league, with the fourth highest average possession, 10 games in.

Pochettino, from a footballing point of view, feels extremely aligned to the values of Ferguson's United, and as a result will implement numerous similarities to the things Carrick wanted, but ultimately failed, to deliver.

His wealth of experience make him a more proven entity than the departing United manager and if he can get his team fit and pressing high, in typically Pochettino fashion, they should see an upturn in form.

Expanding on his managerial approach, while managing Spurs he explained how "the most important thing [was] to create a good shape for players to be comfortable and to show their real qualities".

Rather than relying on pre-defined pattern, he looks to empower individuals to solve attacking problems. Taking this approach means recruitment of top talent matters more than ever.

"He [gave] me the confidence and licence to go where I wanted on the pitch, where I [could] use my strengths," said Cole Palmer, who enjoyed his most productive Premier League season under Pochettino at Chelsea.

United have good attackers but they will need to take the same initiative Palmer did, if platformed to their strengths - something Pochettino does well.

If they don't, and if Pochettino is to stumble, it will likely be in United's inability to break down stubborn defences when asked to dominate the ball - in what would feel like Groundhog Day, again.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field.

GOCE, its name was short for Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer, launched in 2009 on a mission to map Earth's gravity like never before. But despite that successful mission, it was doomed in 2013 when it ran out of fuel.

At the time, controllers weren't sure where GOCE would fall back to Earth. Some people worried that it might crash into a populated area. However, the small spacecraft broke up in the atmosphere and didn't cause any property damage.

It disintegrated about 50 miles above the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. The European Space Agency called the mission a success. GOCE lasted far longer than expected. It showed small variations in Earth's gravity, mapped the structure of Earth's crust and mantle, and tracked ocean currents.

The GOCE satellite was a sleek spacecraft, with fins covered in solar panels that gave it a futuristic design. In fact, its look earned it a pretty cool nickname.

"GOCE's sleek, elegant aerodynamic design — responsible for it being dubbed the 'Ferrari of space' — immediately set it apart from most other satellites,." ESA officials said in a description.

There was more than looks behind GOCE's design. In order to generate the best map ever of Earth's gravitational field, GOCE had to fly in an orbit so low — just 139 miles (224 kilometers) — it needed to counteract the drag from the gossamer thin atmosphere of Earth at that altitude. The International Space Station orbits Earth at nearly twice that altitude.

GOCE was powered by an xenon ion engine that allowed to maintain its low orbit for four years. Once it ran out of fuel, the 1-ton satellite could not maintain its position in space, leading to a fiery plunge to Earth.

The large size of GOCE — it weighed 2,425 pounds (1,100 kilograms) and was 17 feet (5.3 meters) long and 3.2 feet (1 m) wide — made its reentry stand out, particularly since at least 25% of the satellite was expected to reach the Earth's surface.

#783. Jamie Dornan & Anthony Mackie Share Hilarious Lesson From Fatherhood

Jamie Dornan and Anthony Mackie—who are costarring in the thriller series 12 12 12—exclusively told E! News about their kids' reactions to growing up with movie star dads.

Jamie Dornan and Anthony Mackie's most important critics are their kids.

The actors—who first starred in 2019's Synchronic before reuniting for upcoming TV series 12 12 12—confessed that amid their many roles as action stars over the years, earning cool points from their children has been no easy feat.

"If they don't think I'm cool after Lord of the Rings, I'm done," Dornan, who plays Aragorn in the upcoming prequel, The Hunt for Gollum, joked in an exclusive interview with E! News’ Will Marfuggi. "If that's not good enough for my kids, then I don't know what else to offer them."

The 50 Shades of Grey alum brought his three kids Dulcie, 13, Elva, 10 and Alberta, 7, with wife Amelia Warner to stay with him in New Zealand during the fantasy shoot, where they were thankfully impressed by his performance on set.

"Usually, they ask to leave. Like, they come to set, and after half an hour, they're like, 'You're just saying the same thing over and over. This is so boring,'" Dornan admitted. "They came to set one night when I was fighting and beheading orcs and stuff, and they were like, 'It was cool.'"

That said, the 44-year-old was pleased that his little ones found it "good to see Daddy all heroic like that" because, as he put it, "that'll be as cool as it gets for me."

Mackie's brood, on the other hand—which includes four sons with ex-wife Sheletta Chapital—weren't so easily won over by their dad moonlighting as a soldier with supernatural powers, but for good reason. The Captain America actor is already a superhero at home.

"My boys could care less," Mackie remarked with a laugh. "At the end of the day, I realized they just want me to be dad."

And the 48-year-old understands why his family unit is more content with quality time at home, including playing pickleball.

"I love the fact that all they want from me is me," he continued. "But then when I come home, we get to be one big family."

Still, Mackie admitted bringing the crew as his plus-fours to a red carpet was more than a typical 'bring your kids to work' day, even for them.

"They went to the premiere of my movie," Mackie recounted. "They had never seen anything of that scale, like of that magnitude."

And Mackie and Dornan's latest project is yet another grand production. The Marvel alum credited the art department when remarking, "The scale of the show, I feel, is kind of like another character."

The Belfast native agreed the ambitious approach paid off for the series, premiering Nov. 13 on Apple TV, about a meticulously planned fictional robbery of a bank in Zurich.

"It's like the biggest heist in European history," Dornan said, using the British slang for cheap when adding, "It couldn't be pony. It needed to be big."

New episodes drop on Fridays through Dec. 25.

Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy -- which also includes original songs from John Legend & Kamasi Washington -- arrives Friday on Apple TV.

Thanks to 1965’s A Charlie Brown Christmas and its enduring Vince Guaraldi Trio soundtrack, we’ve long associated the Peanuts gang with Christmas. Now, Snoopy is getting in on the yuletide action with Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy, which arrives Friday (Nov. 13) on Apple TV — and Billboard Family has an exclusive clip that features Laufey‘s new cover of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas.” Related Could Jason & Travis Kelce Judge 'DWTS'? Taylor Swift's Backup Dancer Thinks It'd Be 'Incredible' 'Thursday Night Football' 2026: How to Watch Washington Commanders vs. New York Giants Live Online Here's How to Watch 'Southern Charm' Season 12 Online for Free Explore Laufey See latest videos, charts and news

Laufey’s jazz sensibilities are the perfect addition to the Peanuts musical canon, with her warm vocals bringing a cozy Christmas glow to the snowy clip. In Billboard‘s exclusive preview, we see the gang sledding down a snow-dusted hill — some using gift boxes or wreaths as their sleighs — as well as Schroeder playing his red piano under a Beethoven-topped Christmas tree, Marcie and Peppermint Patty decorating an ornate gingerbread house, and Lucy reading bedtime stories to Linus and Rerun in matching PJs.

In the new special, Snoopy lands on Santa’s naughty list — but as we learn at the end of the Laufey-soundtracked clip, the beagle finds his way off just in time to get a new hockey stick so he can hit the ice with Woodstock and the rest of the birds.

“Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas” was originally written for the 1944 movie musical Meet Me in St. Louis by Hugh Martin and Ralph Blane and performed by Judy Garland in the film. It has been covered countless times since, including by Frank Sinatra, the Carpenters, Michael Bublé, Christina Aguilera and Garland’s daughter Lorna Luft.

12 Days of Snoopy is produced by Peanuts and WildBrain and is executive produced by Josh Scherba, Stephanie Betts, Logan McPherson, Paige Braddock, Chris Bracco and Mark Evestaff.

#781. Special Forces Season 5 Finale: 3 Celebrity Winners Revealed

Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test crowned Candace Cameron Bure, Collin Gosselin and Alexia Umansky the season five winners, the celebrities outlasting the final competition.

These celebrities have proven they’re the world’s toughest.

While there were seven finalists heading into the Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test season five finale on Nov. 12, only three proved they truly had what it takes to win.

And those winners were: Candace Cameron Bure, Collin Gosselin and Alexia Umansky, who faced what one series staff sergeant called “12 hours of absolute hell” in order to ensure their victory.

The three winners, as well as boxer Alycia Baumgardner, French celebrity David Charvet, comedian Hannah Stocking and NBA alum Matt Barnes’ final challenge involved 12 hours of simulated interrogation after the finalists were “captured behind enemy lines.” They were tasked with devising and maintaining cover stories, building rapport and acting human with their captors, all while making it to the very end through hours of intense interrogation, the downtime of which they were kept in rooms with hoods on.

Baumgardner eventually pulled herself out of the challenge when the pressure became too much, Charvet was removed for failing to build rapport with his captors and Stocking and Barnes failed when interrogators were able to debunk their cover stories.

That left Jon & Kate Plus 8’s Gosselin, Umansky—who started the competition with her dad Mauricio Umansky—and Full House alum Bure, who proved they had what it took to win.

For Umansky, she shared how happy she was to bring home the win for her and her dad, adding she got through the toughest moments by keeping her eye on the prize.

“I have visualized what it’s like to walk out of this as a winner,” she said during a confessional. “I think I just have to keep that picture in my head so strong.”

Meanwhile, Bure felt her victory to have an impact beyond herself.

“This one’s for all the women out there,” she said through tears after winning. “No matter what challenges you have, physically you can do it.”

And for Gosselin—who is estranged from his mother Kate Gosselin and many of seven siblings, an ordeal he chronicles in his recently-released memoir—this show proved he was capable after previously being discharged from the Marines, which he alleges was orchestrated by his mother.

Through tears, the 22-year-old said, “Now I feel I have this new profound belief in myself that nobody can take away from me.”

But while Umansky, Gosselin and Bure are reveling in their win, read on for a look back at all the celebrities who pushed themselves during season five.

In any respectable audiobook project, finding the names of Andy Weir ("The Martian," "Project Hail Mary") and Benjamin Percy ("The Ninth Metal," "Wolverine") attached would elicit intense fan interest, but add the superstar vocal talents of Anthony Mackie ("Avengers: Infinity War," "Avengers: Doomsday"), Ariana DeBose ("West Side Story"), and John Leguizamo ("Ice Age"), and it catapults this sonic odyssey into the stratosphere.

Such is the case with "Exoplanet," Audible Original’s new 7-episode science fiction audio drama executive produced by Weir and penned by Percy. Its planet-hopping space disaster narrative sees the crew of the starship Wild Blue Yonder hit a quantum anomaly, forcing their ship to crash-land onto a deadly exoplanet. All is not as it seems, though, as each crew member arrives in a different era on the same world.

We hooked up with Mackie, DeBose, and Lequizamo to learn more about this renaissance of audio dramas and what attracted them to board Weir's sci-fi thriller.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Mackie voices Chief Engineer Jeff Shaw. His attraction to the imaginative genre began at an early age thanks to some cool family friends while growing up in the Big Easy.

"My brother went to college at Morehouse," he tells SPACE. "I was like 8, and he was 18. He’d always bring friends home, because New Orleans is a party city, so they'd come over and get drunk. But one of his friends gave me a book by Walter Mosley and one by Octavia Butler, and I got hooked into sci-fi and the future."

"From 'Back to the Future' to 'Aliens,' the future was such an idea of what was going to be out there. Now we’re living it," reveals Mackie. "It’s very important to me as a human being to have that construct as a part of my career. The only thing more arrogant than wanting to be president is standing up and saying, 'Yeah, I can go to space.' That sounds crazy to me."

Leguizamo's New York City childhood was influenced by absorbing classic radio dramas of the past, which primed him for this special Audible project.

“It was Anthony and Ariana being in it that really pumped me up, and of course Andy Weir," he recalls regarding his portrayal of Science Officer Logan Bowers. "Then when I got the theme, that it was something relevant today and makes you think about computers and technology taking over and making us obsolete. It just hit me in that right zeitgeist, at that right little point."

"As a poor kid, there was no YouTube or cell phones, and we didn’t have computers," reminisces Leguizamo. "I used to go to the Broadcast Museum on 53rd Street and listen to old radio plays like The Shadow and these incredible detective radio plays. It's a different art form. With no visuals, your voice has to create the world. I thought that was an incredible challenge."

DeBose portrays the Wild Blue Yonder's confident First Officer Becca Bang, who’s stranded in a temporal mystery that might engulf her at any moment.

"I've yet to do anything like this, which is always exciting," she adds. "I was a little afraid of it, which told me I should do it. These gents are so talented. It's great company. It’s coming from brilliant minds who build worlds so impeccably. And it's about real stuff we’re dealing with today. I liked the idea that we could tell this story and make people listen and create a space for them to imagine themselves in it and see how they problem-solve to make the world a bit better."

Recording your character's lines is far more difficult than just stepping up to the microphone to read a script, and our ace "Exoplanet" trio delivered in every session.

"I just go in and throw myself at something," DeBose recalls. "I don’t really have a method. But I can tell you this: it is a full-body workout. I use everything at my disposal, whether it’s a chair or a pillow or running in place. I just do what the character does and end up sweating. And after three days, I have to go sit in silence. It's great. I love the idea of bringing back the radio play. The art of listening is such a thing. I don’t think people listen enough. Even for myself."

Likewise, Leguizamo embraced his booth sessions with exuberance and authenticity.

"You have to cancel the rest of your day, especially if you've got to talk, because your vocal chords are fried," he admits. "And if they're not fried you're not doing your job. You really have to do the physicality. If you run you have to run like a maniac and be out of breath. If I'm getting hit I start punching myself. Then there’s a sexiness to doing these things. Your voice has to have a little mystery, a little naughtiness. It’s an interesting intersection where you pull it back a little and invite the audience in.”

For Mackie, who’s used to athleticism needed to play MCU superheroes like The Falcon and Captain America, recording dialogue offered a different type of opportunity.

“I look for reasons not to talk to people, so I love doing these," he jokes. "Once I’m out of the studio, I’m not talking to anybody for two days. At a certain point for me, I find mentally I get tired of hearing myself talk. I just have to come home at cut off. I’ve said enough words for the next month.”

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

#778. How Hailey Bieber, Justin Bieber's Son Is Following in Dad's Footsteps

Hailey Bieber shared a new clip of her and Justin Bieber's son Jack Blues, 2, following in his footsteps by playing with a keyboard.

That's Hailey Bieber and Justin Bieber's baby, he's iconic.

The Rhode Beauty founder shared a new video of her and Justin's son Jack Blues, 2, that revealed he may already be following in the "Sorry" singer's footsteps when it comes to music.

Hailey posted a quick clip of her son on her Instagram Stories Nov. 12, showing him being mesmerized by a keyboard as he plays with the keys. In fact, zooms in on Jack's fingers in the video taken from the couch behind him as he leans against a coffee table and plays his tune while wearing a salmon-colored sweatsuit.

She wrote over the video that "blues loves the keys."

Jack's apparent penchant for music shouldn't come as a surprise, of course. The pint-sized tot has gotten a front row seat to his dad's music career, like when he cheered Justin on as he prepared for his headlining set at Coachella this spring—even rocking a temporary Bieberchella tattoo.

SpaceX is one big step closer to the 15th test flight of its Starship megarocket.

The company announced today (Nov. 10) that it had moved its latest Starship first stage, known as Super Heavy Booster 22, to the launch mount at its Starbase facility in South Texas ahead of Flight 15, which is scheduled to lift off this Friday (Nov. 13).

During the upcoming launch test, SpaceX plans to catch both Booster 22 and Starship's Ship upper stage with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms in a double landing catch — something the private spaceflight company has never tried before. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history.

Booster 22 therefore "was used for final catch testing upon arrival [at the pad], including a suspended squeeze test at catch height," SpaceX said in an X post today (Nov. 10).

That post shared four photos of the giant booster, which is powered by 33 of SpaceX's next-gen Raptor engines. The first shot showed Super Heavy in one of Starbase's "Mega Bay" assembly buildings before rollout, while the other three depicted it grasped by the tower's arms, held high in the South Texas sky.

SpaceX has used the chopstick arms during Starship flights before; it has successfully caught Super Heavy on three separate occasions. But the company has never attempted a catch of Ship, which flies higher and farther than the booster and is therefore a more challenging target. And SpaceX only reached orbit with Starship for the first time on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28.

So Flight 15 will break new ground. And, if all goes to plan, it will give us a look at the future: SpaceX plans to catch Super Heavy and Ship on all operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will allow the company to boost the megarocket's launch cadence.

And SpaceX wants to fly Starship incredibly often, so that it can build out its Starlink V3 broadband constellation and even bigger Starmind AI data-center network. Indeed, Elon Musk has said the company is eyeing 10,000 Starship flights per year by 2030.

If all goes to plan, Flight 15 will launch from Starbase on Friday during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time).

Super Heavy will return to Starbase for its catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff. Ship will follow suit much later — about 22 hours later, in fact, after it has deployed 26 Starlink V3 spacecraft into LEO and completed 14 circuits of our planet.

You can watch all the action live here at Space.com and get updates about the mission here.

#774. HUNTR/X Hitting the Road for 2027 KPop Demon Hunters Golden World Tour: See Dates

Animated characters Rumi, Mira and Zoey will come to life in the show that will also feature live-action stunts and performers and fan-favorite songs.

KPop Demon Hunters is jumping from the screen to the stage. The wildly popular Netflix animated movie will hit the road in 2027 for the Kpop Demon Hunters Golden World tour, slated to kick off on June 4 in Baltimore, Md. and crisscross North America with shows in Chicago, Pittsburgh, Atlanta, Orlando, Dallas, Phoenix, Los Angeles and Las Vegas before hopping to Europe and the U.K. for shows in the fall.

The tour is currently slated to wind down on Oct. 22-23 with three shows at The O2 in London.

A release announcing the dates promised that it will feature the movie’s beloved songs and bring to life the film’s three animated stars, Rumi, Mira and Zoey. They will, “ interact with the audience through cutting-edge performance innovations that bring this fan-favorite K-pop girl group to life like never before,” according to the release, which notes that their fellow animated co-stars, the Saja Boys and Derpy Tiger, will also make appearances.

“Every fan in attendance will play a part to show the world How It’s Done, Done, Done!” the release continued. “More than a concert, this is a first-of-its-kind production that immerses fans in the storytelling with live-action stunts and performers, fan-favorite music and choreography and special performances.”

The movie’s breakout hit single, “Golden,” performed by the fictional group HUNTR/X and sung by real-life vocalists EJAE, Audrey Nuna and REI AMI, spent eight weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The soundtrack also made history after it became the first to generate four simultaneous Hot 100 top 10 hits with “Golden,” “Soda Pop,” “Your Idol” and “How It’s Done.”

Presented by Netflix and AEG Presents, the tour — which will announce additional international stops in Asia and Latin America at a later date — will hit nearly 50 cities for 150 performances in 2027 and 2028. Tickets go on sale to the general public on Nov. 20 at 10 a.m. local time; click here for details. There will also be a Mastercard presale beginning on Nov. 18 at 10 a.m. local time, as well as a FOR THE FANS presale beginning on Nov. 19 at 10 a.m. local time.

“KPop Demon Hunters has transformed from a breakout hit into a generational phenomenon — sustaining 63 consecutive weeks in Netflix’s Global Top 10, eclipsing 2 billion Spotify streams for ‘Golden’ and breaking the all-time record for the longest running soundtrack at No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Soundtracks chart,” said Netflix’s chief marketing officer, Marian Lee, in a statement. “This fandom was never about a single moment, and the Golden World Tour is how we keep it going – bringing that ‘Takedown’ energy to arenas around the world, where fans can sing, dance and help HUNTR/X seal the Honmoon.”

Rich Schaefer, president of global touring for AEG Presents added, “KPop Demon Hunters has become a global phenomenon, with characters and music that already mean so much to fans around the world. We’re excited to work with Netflix to bring that world to life on tour, with the music at the heart of a show that makes fans part of the adventure. The Golden World Tour gives us the chance to create something special for this incredible audience and bring fans of every generation together to experience it.”

SpaceX will make history with the world's first full recovery of an orbital rocket on Starship Flight 15. Here's when to watch.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX is just days away from what might be its most ambitious test flight yet of the company's massive Starship megarocket, the largest launch vehicle ever built.

On Friday (Nov. 13), SpaceX will launch its next Starship test flight on a mission that, if successful, will return both its Super Heavy first-stage booster and Ship upper stage to Earth for back-to-back landings at their launch pad. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history. And if you want to watch it live, you'll need to know what time and where to tune in.

In our guide below, we'll explain exactly when and how to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission. It is the 15th test flight of the giant stainless-steel reusable rocket, which SpaceX wants to use for everything from Starlink internet satellite launches to landing NASA Artemis astronauts on the moon in 2028, and even for a crewed flight to Mars. But first, SpaceX has to successfully recover and refly both stages, something it's never done before — and that's where Flight 15 comes in. It's the first time the company will try to land an entire Starship rocket. Here's when to tune in.

The Starship Flight 15 test mission is currently scheduled to launch no earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. But there is a chance of a later liftoff time.

SpaceX has said it has a 75-minute window in which to launch Starship Flight 15 to add some flexibility into its preflight countdown. That means the launch could take place anytime between 5:45 p.m. and 7 p.m. EST (2245-0000 Nov. 14). The local time for the launch window will be 4:45 p.m. to 6 p.m. CST.

SpaceX has not formally announced if it has backup days for the launch, but if the company does have those options, liftoff would likely occur at the same time, based on past Starship missions that saw delays.

One thing that separates Starship Flight 15 from past Starship test flights is its length. The mission, if it runs its full duration, will last just over 22.5 hours until Ship lands back at Starbase. That landing would occur on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 4:17 p.m. EST (2117 GMT). If SpaceX launches at the end of its window on Friday, at 7 p.m. EST, the Ship landing would occur on Saturday at 5:32 p.m. EST (2232 GMT).

Meanwhile, the Super Heavy, known as Booster 22, will land about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

Related: Read our SpaceX Starship and Super Heavy guide for a detailed look at the megarocket.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

Yes, you'll be able to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch online, and you have many ways to do so.

Space.com will host a livestream simulcast of Starship Flight 15 on this page, as well as on our homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace. That webcast will begin about 30 minutes before liftoff, at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT).

SpaceX, of course, will offer its own Starship Flight 15 livestream on its Flight 15 mission page, as well as on its X account. That livestream will also begin 30 minutes before launch, at 5:15 p.m. EST (it's the same one as on Space.com).

If you need your Starship launch preparations fix before the Nov. 13 launch, good news: You can see SpaceX's prep work live online.

NASASpaceflight's YouTube channel offers live views of SpaceX's Starship pads at Starbase 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

On Wednesday (Nov. 11), the channel will stream live views of the Starship Flight 15 rocket stacking, starting at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT).

The NASASpaceflight Flight 15 launch webcast will begin on Nov. 13 at 11:45 a.m. EDT (1645 GMT), about six hours before launch. NASASpaceflight typically offers live commentary and constantly changing views of the Starship launch pad via remote cameras positioned around Starbase.

If there was ever a SpaceX Starship test flight to see in person, this just might be it.

In addition to watching the world's largest rocket launch into space, Starship Flight 15 offers the chance to see both parts of that megarocket return to Earth and be caught in mid-air, 22 hours apart.

If you've read our past Starship launch viewing guides, you'll know that SpaceX doesn't have an official viewing site for Starship launches. But you can see the spectacle from several public beaches (as well as private campgrounds). Cameron County Amphitheater at Isla Blanca Park on South Padre Island is always my first recommendation (I watched the first Starship launch from there in April 2023). The park offers a clear view of the Starship launch site across the bay and includes views of boats on the water. There are also bathrooms close by for your convenience. It's 5 miles (8 kilometers) from the launch site as the crow flies. But plan to head out early as traffic can be heavy, especially if you have to cross the bridge from Port Isabel.

Speaking of Port Isabel, there are stretches along Highway 48 between Port Isabel and Brownsville, Texas where you can pull over to the shoulder to watch the launch from 6 to 8 miles (10 to 13 km) away. But it's just the side of a highway, so don't expect bathrooms there. The website SpaceLaunchSchedule.com does report that there are "open pull-offs" to park, from which you can get "wide wetland views." And, of course, it's free. I've driven along Highway 48 during two Starbase visits but have not pulled over to the shoulder to test this site.

If you're on the Mexico side of the border, you may be able to watch Starship Flight 15 from Playa Bagdad, a public beach with a "head-on view of the launch tower and a festive vibe," according to SpaceLaunchSchedule.com.

Finally, there is the Rocket Ranch campground, where you can get a closer view of Starship launches — but you have to pay $200 a ticket (kids under age 17 are $40). The ranch is 3.8 miles (6.1 km) from the Starbase launch site, and your ticket allows you to camp there for one day and one night. Longer four-day stay packages are available.

The Rocket Ranch has two primary viewing locations: The "Outpost" offers the closest view and "unmatched media service," so you can stay connected. The second location is a bit farther away on the campground itself. Please note: Tickets include bus transportation from the ranch campground to a viewing site and back, but it is for one launch attempt only. Be sure to read the full Rocket Ranch FAQ for details on the site.

If everything goes to plan, SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 orbital launch and landing test could last up to 22.5 hours and orbit the Earth 14 times.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in a mission overview.

But the test flight could end early. That's what happened on SpaceX's first orbital Starship test mission, Flight 14 on Sept. 28, which was expected to last nearly 10 hours and orbit Earth six times. Instead, SpaceX ended the mission after three hours and two orbits of Earth as a safety precaution.

"Starship’s initial return to launch site mission is expected to orbit the Earth at an altitude of ~275 km and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet over the course of a more than 22-hour flight," SpaceX wrote in the mission description. "Similar to Starship’s first orbital mission, the flight profile has been designed with the opportunity to insert into a passively safe suborbital trajectory or safely deorbit at multiple pre-determined areas over the ocean after raising to an orbital altitude."

Super Heavy liquid methane loading begins

Raptor engine chilldown begins on Ship and Super Heavy

Liftoff ("Excitement Guaranteed," SpaceX says)

Hot-staging separation/Ship Raptor engine ignition

Super Heavy boostback burn engine shutdown

Super Heavy landing burn shutdown (followed by 'chopsticks" catch)

Starship orbital insertion engine burn begins

If SpaceX has to end the Starship Flight 15 test flight early, it has three primary splashdown zones to land the Ship upper stage in the ocean.

The company could drop the Ship vehicle in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Hawaii in early and late stages of the mission, according to a reentry overview. A mid-mission splashdown window off the coast of Chile is available if needed at that time. A late-mission splashdown zone in the Gulf of Mexico is also available.

The Gulf is also a wave-off splashdown zone for SpaceX's Starship Super Heavy Booster 22 in case it is unable to land shortly after liftoff.

As with Starship Flight 14, SpaceX is loading Flight 15 with 26 operational Starlink V3 internet satellites. They will be deployed in orbit within the first 90 minutes of the flight.

"The Starship upper stage’s primary objectives include the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites and the first return to launch site and catch at Starbase," SpaceX wrote in its overview. "Starship will only execute a return to launch site if the flight control team has ensured that the vehicle systems critical for reentry maneuvers and final landing burn and tower approach are healthy."

While SpaceX is hoping to launch Starship Flight 15 on time, there is a chance that a technical issue or bad weather could prevent liftoff on Nov. 13.

SpaceX has not announced any official backup days for the Starship Flight 15 launch, but it is likely that the company has at least one if not two additional opportunities to try again, based on past Starship launches. Any backup launch attempts will depend greatly on the nature of a launch delay.

A good website to watch is the official Starbase page for Boca Chica Beach and Highway 4 closure alerts here. Those beach closures can be a good indicator of SpaceX's available flight windows.

You'll be able to follow SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission on Space.com as it happens. Be sure to come back on launch day for complete Starship Flight 15 coverage.

The Seestar S30 Plus is a great beginner smart telescope for deep-sky imaging, along with a reasonable price tag and enough features to develop your astro skills without buying another instrument.

Excellent deep-sky imaging, even with light pollution

Built-in filters and easy automated set-up

Lower resolution than more expensive smart telescopes

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I’ve used several smart telescopes over the last few years, but I'd recommend the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus to almost anyone wanting to get started in astrophotography. At $499/€499, it’s a complete imaging system that can photograph galaxies, nebulae and star clusters automatically, even from a light-polluted city. Better still, it’s so small that it can live on a bookshelf.

I recently captured images of the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Pleiades (M45) with the S30 Plus. All were remarkably easy to capture, and none of the images accompanying this review required external processing. It’s basically point-and-shoot astrophotography — if you live under light-polluted skies, that’s a game-changer.

I also think the S30 Plus makes an ideal companion to a conventional optical telescope. I can set it to photograph a nebula I have no hope of seeing under light pollution while I try to find brighter objects through the eyepiece of another telescope. It will then get on with collecting photons while I enjoy observing.

For anyone who already owns a telescope but doesn’t want the expense and complexity of conventional astrophotography, that’s a compelling proposition.

One problem with buying a cheap optical telescope is that deep-sky objects rarely resemble the colorful photographs you see online. The moon, planets and bright star clusters can look wonderful through an eyepiece, but faint galaxies and nebulas are much harder to appreciate, particularly from a town or city.

Like all smart telescopes, the S30 Plus gets around that problem by photographing objects rather than showing them directly. Its camera takes repeated exposures, which the telescope automatically stacks to reduce noise and gradually reveal faint detail. The longer you leave it working, the better the resulting image tends to become.

Being able to photograph colorful nebulas without traveling to a remote observing site is one of the biggest attractions of the S30 Plus. For beginners living in cities, it could transform their experience of astronomy.

I’ve always preferred spending my nights looking at the sky rather than fiddling with equipment, which is one reason I enjoy smart telescopes. Traditional astrophotography can involve a camera, tracking mount, adapters, cables, alignment, a laptop and considerable patience before the first useful exposure begins. The S30 Plus removes almost all of that.

I can put it outside, connect the Seestar app and choose a target from its built-in sky atlas. The telescope then moves to the correct position, identifies the star field, centers the object, focuses and begins imaging. Within minutes, a photograph starts appearing on my smartphone. That leaves me free to use an optical telescope alongside it — or stay inside and do something else.

Using the S30 Plus’s built-in UV/IR cut filter — which blocks ultraviolet and infrared light — I captured the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), a popular deep-sky object. As the hours went by, the dust lanes on its outskirts appeared in ever more detail. That’s how smart telescopes work — they collect and combine dozens or hundreds of short exposures, gradually revealing fainter structure while reducing noise.

So impressive is the image after only about five or six exposures that it’s tempting to stop after a few minutes — but patience makes an enormous difference. Fortunately, you don’t have to stand beside the S30 Plus. You can leave it collecting light — even overnight, thanks to its scheduling option (though it’s not waterproof, so check the weather forecast!).

Using the dual-band anti-light pollution filter, the Pleiades open cluster (M45) provided another interesting test. The S30 Plus has a mosaic mode that photographs overlapping sections of sky to create a larger image than its main camera can capture in a single frame. It’s ideal for expansive targets such as the Pleiades and Andromeda, although gathering enough exposures takes time. The app shows how much of the mosaic has been completed, and if needs be, you can continue collecting data on subsequent nights.

I also photographed the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884) and the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules (M13), both relatively swift targets, but as anyone who’s used a smart telescope knows, it’s the faint nebulas that are the real prize. For those, dark skies mean better data — and that’s exactly why a smart telescope needs to be portable.

The S30 Plus weighs just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg) and measures 8.25 x 5.5 x 3.15 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm) when switched off. That’s small enough to fit into a camera bag in place of another lens or camera body, which is a major advantage because I travel to remote locations quite frequently. That fact that it sits on such a tiny tripod is also a boon.

I’ve recently used the much larger Seestar S50 Pro, which weighs 6.17 lbs (2.8 kg). It’s a more capable imaging instrument with a 50mm aperture and a larger 8.3-megapixel sensor, but its heavier, bulkier chassis is harder to get into carry-on luggage. The S30 Plus and the higher-spec S30 Pro also differ from the S50 Pro in that they come with a padded carry case. This has a useful carrying handle, although there’s no shoulder strap or dedicated storage for the tripod and magnetic solar filter.

It’s also worth taking along a portable battery and USB-C cable to recharge its built-in 6,000mAh battery during long sessions, though it lasts about six hours, which will suit most observing sessions.

The original, now-discontinued S30 was already impressive, but the S30 Plus is a substantial upgrade. It has improved four-element apochromatic optics with ED glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras, each producing 1,440x2,560-pixel images. That’s almost 80% more pixels than the original S30’s main camera.

The main camera’s field of view has increased slightly to about three degrees, while the wide-angle camera now covers 43.5 degrees of sky. The latter can be used for star trails, though I suspect it’s something most people will experiment with occasionally.

There’s also an EQ mode. This will align the telescope with Earth’s rotation to allow longer exposures and sharper edges, which I found worked really well. It requires an appropriately angled mount or wedge (such as the Seestar TH10 Fluid Tripod Head) and a small tripod.

I tested it at 51 degrees north, which randomly appears to be the cut-off point for ease of use because of the tilt it puts on the telescope. It’s when a tripod begins to topple with the weight, meaning you need a tripod whose legs can be set at a low angle (Seestar’s TC20 tripod would be ideal, and is very compact).

The app makes it all very easy to set up, and advanced imaging possibilities like this are welcome. So, too, is the option of outputting images as lossless FITS files for anyone wanting to process their images using specialist software.

That’s what makes the Seestar S30 Plus such a good beginner’s telescope. It’s easy to use immediately, but there’s plenty of scope to develop more sophisticated astrophotography skills without buying another instrument.

The S30 Plus isn’t limited to deep-sky photography. I photographed a near-full moon against a blue daytime sky, something I particularly enjoy doing with smart telescopes because they’re so quick to set up.

It also comes with a magnetic white-light solar filter, allowing safe photographs of the sun when the filter is securely fitted. This must always be installed before pointing the telescope towards the sun. I did have to manually guide the S30 Plus to the sun and moon on a few occasions, but it’s easy enough to do, and I actually like the option to manually take control — few other smart telescopes allow it. Once you’ve found the sun or moon, the scope centers it and keeps it in view (unless you’re on a moving ship, by the way, where tracking generally fails — something for eclipse chasers to think about).

Planetary photography is less impressive. The 30mm aperture and short focal length aren’t ideal for detailed views of Jupiter or Saturn, so for anyone primarily interested in observing and imaging planets, I’d recommend a conventional optical telescope instead.

The S30 Plus occupies an interesting position in ZWO’s increasingly crowded Seestar range. With dual 8.3MP cameras and wider fields of view, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade from the original S30. Meanwhile, the $999 S50 Pro has a larger 50mm aperture that collects almost three times as much light, although it’s also significantly bulkier and more expensive.

Alternatives exist outside ZWO’s range. DwarfLab’s Dwarf Mini is exceptionally portable, but its lower resolution and more limited capabilities make it less versatile. At the other extreme, Unistellar’s Odyssey has an 85mm aperture, an electronic eyepiece and opportunities to contribute to citizen science projects, but it sits in a different price bracket.

The S30 Plus will hit the sweet spot for many. It offers almost everything a beginner needs to explore deep-sky astrophotography, with built-in filters, mosaic mode and EQ tracking giving plenty of advanced features to grow into. Crucially, it’s small enough to travel with easily. Yes, you can spend more and get slightly better image data, but most beginners don’t need to.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the most affordable smart telescopes available, but it’s also one of the best-value offerings in its class.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.
