#769. ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Goes Back to (Before) the Beginning With Its 600th Episode

Showrunner Michele Fazekas breaks down Christopher Meloni's return and the state of the Benson-Stabler relationship.

[This story contains spoilers from the 600th episode of Law & Order: SVU.]

Law & Order: SVU reached a huge milestone Thursday: 600 episodes, a number that only two scripted primetime shows have ever hit before. The cast and crew celebrated with a cake on set during filming and a dinner afterward — and then went back to work. Six hundred episodes is an extremely rare feat for a scripted series (The Simpsons and Gunsmoke are the only ones with more), but Thursday’s episode was also the sixth of season 28; 15 more are still to come. Related Stories Business Fanatics Studios' Next Big Media Play Is the NBA All-Star Game TV Jason Benetti Will Replace Dan Hicks on Notre Dame Play-by-Play Saturday Following Sudden Passing (Exclusive)

“That’s just doing television,” showrunner Michele Fazekas told The Hollywood Reporter. “It’s our 600th episode, but it’s also just an episode within 21 episodes [this season]. You’re working on five episodes at the same time at any given moment — you’re in prep on some episodes, you’re writing on some episodes, you’re in post on some episodes. Nothing changed in that regard.”

Titled “Obedience,” the 600th episode brings Elliot Stabler (Christopher Meloni) back to the Special Victims Unit after jury consultant Gwen Sharpe (J. Smith-Cameron, who also appeared in the season premiere) convinces Benson (Mariska Hargitay) to take another look at an old case. Gwen is convinced the man in prison for the crime, the rape and murder of a young nun in 1998, is innocent.

Stabler is reluctant to revisit the case — with good reason, it turns out. He failed to follow a couple of leads that could have pointed to the real culprit, a now-retired priest who led mass at the convent where the victim lived. He also cut Benson out of the interrogation in the case, which she went along with at the time because she was new to the squad. The case stirs up complicated feelings in the former partners; when Stabler asks Benson why she’s so interested in digging up the case, she retorts, “Why aren’t you?”

He eventually agrees to work with her, and the pair head upstate to question people who knew the victim (most notably, guest stars Laura Innes and Kathleen Chalfant) and track down the priest.

Fazekas, who wrote the episode (Brenna Malloy directed), said she wanted to give the 600th show the feel of “an old school Benson and Stabler episode” while also looking at the people they have become in the years since. To that end, the episode’s final scenes will give viewers plenty to discuss.

Fazekas unpacked those scenes, the reasons for going back to the show’s early days and more in an interview with THR.

Given the milestone that this is, was there extra planning that went into it? Or did you have ideas on the board for longer than you might normally?

Probably a little bit. I think I had an idea early on in the in the season of what I wished to do, and one of the first things was saying, “Can we bring back Chris Meloni?” Assuming that this is the last centennial episode that we were going to have, it feels like if we could do it, this would be the time to do it. So yeah, there were some earlier ideas than your typical running around trying to figure out what an episode is.

Having Stabler come back into the squad was always part of the plan, then?

It was for me. There were a lot of things that had to happen in order for that to become a reality, including Chris having to be available — he’s busy. But he was. I also knew early on — because I was on the show the first time around, seasons three through seven — I wanted to kind of go back a little bit to an old school Benson and Stabler episode of SVU and honor that era of the show. I just had an idea, and I don’t usually come up with ideas this way, but I was like, “I want it to be a road show.” I want them to be in a car, driving long distances and hashing stuff out. I didn’t know what [the reason] was. I always find that interesting, just putting two people in a place where they can’t get away, and then they have to hash out their stuff.

The structure of SVU is such that cases usually get cleared and some sort of justice is served by the end of the hour. I thought it was really interesting that this one is built on something that they got wrong initially. Why did you want to come at it that way?

In part, it was because you have to explain why are we bringing Detective Stabler back. He doesn’t work in SVU anymore. He works in a completely different department. So what would be big enough that he would come back? It felt sort of organic for it to be an old case, but it’s a case that actually predates the show. The show starts in 1999, and this case is from 1998.

What was not planned but came out in the in the breaking of the story is they were such different people back then. Benson was really new, and Stabler was the senior detective, and she has evolved so much because, at the end of the day, we’re still telling the story of Benson. It fits really nicely into what we’re doing with her character this season, and it made sense for why he’s back. But it also goes to wanting to do and old school SVU episodes, but let’s go back to before SVU was even a thing.

I was also struck by Stabler admitting to Benson that his Catholicism might have blinded him to who the real perpetrator was. His religion has been a thread throughout the character’s run, but I think it’s always interesting when it comes up explicitly in relation to a case.

Chris Meloni was a big proponent of that as well. I think allowing your own preconceptions biases you; it goes to that whole issue [of blind spots] generally. Anybody who was raised Catholic, you think of it as one thing, and it’s very hard for people to accept that this thing that you think is one way has a really dark side. At that time [in 1998], it would have been really hard for Stabler to even understand.

You were on the show for a good portion of the Benson-Stabler partnership during your first tenure, and now you’re back as showrunner. What’s your read on their relationship?

My read is Stabler still has work to do on himself that Benson has done. Benson has evolved in a way, and I love them together, and I love them as partners and as scene partners. But I think part of this episode is talking about how she, in some ways, has moved on from the struggles back then. I think Stabler is still working on it. Stabler is still doing a lot of the same things that he did 20 years ago, and he’s starting to realize, oh, I need to change that.

And given what goes on between them in this episode — arguing about work and life, and then him inviting her to come to Arizona for a while — what do you think the audience’s read is going to be?

Listen, I do think they love each other. I think they both know. I think when he says, “Hey, you want to come to Arizona?” he knows her answer is going to be no. It’s easy to ask that question when you know the answer is no. I don’t think he didn’t mean it, but he also knew what her answer was going to be, and I think now is not the time. Is there time down the line? Maybe, but I think he’s got some work to do. She can have some work to do as well, but I think she’s probably a little further down that path than he is.

I’ve always thought that they love each other in a way that sort of transcends a sexual relationship. They deeply love each other, and they’ve acknowledged that before, and I think this sort of reinforces it. But I also think he knows I’ve got more to do with myself.

Where are you in terms of production now?

We are shooting episode 10 and in prep on episode 11.

Anything you can say about the next few episodes?

We have a nice little arc going of that we started at the beginning of the season that we continue, where the cases that they’re faced with are messy and don’t have easy answers. Benson is really struggling with feeling like nothing has changed. No matter how hard we work, sometimes it doesn’t matter. I like the idea of pushing her — the episode we’re shooting now and the next episode are pushing her to the edges of not even what is legal, but what is ethically and morally right to do, because she’s starting to not care.

The episode we’re shooting right now, the bad guy is so bad. We’re talking about “Why is he doing what he’s doing?” And she actually says, “I don’t care,” which is a big thing for her. But you also understand it because the guy is such a bad guy.

Anything you can say about how Stephanie March re-enters the show as Alex Cabot?

Benson goes to her and asks for help. They didn’t end things on a totally happy note the last time she was on the show, but Benson goes back to her.

Is Alex still doing the same sort of work she was that last time?

#768. NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events

The UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermaths of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.

The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.

UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement.

"The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement.

UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV."

UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light.

"In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find."

UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars, however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas.

Supernovas occur when a massive star runs out of fuel for nuclear fusion and can no longer support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the core of the star collapses, its outer layers are blasted outward in cosmic explosions we call supernovas.

This is a process that scientists are keen to understand, as these explosions fling the heavy elements forged during the stars' lifetimes into surrounding galaxies. This material becomes the building blocks of the next generation of stars, planets, and possibly even life.

UVEX will also investigate what happens to the end products of some supernovas, neutron stars, when they meet and merge.

Neutron stars contain between one and two times the mass of the sun crammed into a width of around 12 miles (20 kilometers). That means they are composed of matter so dense that, if a teaspoon of it were brought to Earth, it would weigh over 1 billion tons. That's equivalent to stacking around 9 million adult blue whales on a spoon.

So, when neutron stars in binary systems spiral together and merge, they create an environment so violent that it's the only place in the universe where scientists are sure that elements heavier than lead, like gold, silver, and platinum, are able to be forged.

Currently, neutron star mergers are detected via ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves. Scientists can then follow up on the aftermath of the mergers by observing them in electromagnetic light, from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy radio waves. Thus, UVEX will add another aspect to the investigation of neutron star collisions and our understanding of where heavy elements originate.

The new space telescope's maneuverability will allow it to observe these explosive events very shortly after they happen, giving it an advantage over other instruments, including NASA's long-serving Hubble Space Telescope.

"With UVEX, we will now be able to follow up on gravitational-wave events in ultraviolet light," UVEX team member and Caltech scientist Mansi Kasliwal said in the same statement. "I can count on two hands how many spectra we have of transient events in their infancy phase with the Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble is, of course, amazing and does have some ultraviolet capabilities, but it cannot rapidly pivot to observe real-time events."

UVEX will also be revolutionary in the study of blue stars that have had their outer layers of hydrogen stripped away by companion stars. These stars offer researchers a unique opportunity to study the interior of stars, which is usually obscured by their outer layers.

"We will be able to see what's inside the stars," Kareem El-Badry, an associate professor of astronomy at Caltech and a member of the UVEX team, said in the same statement. "We only know of a small number of stripped stars of this type now. UVEX will find hundreds."

All of the above elements discussed are the expected discoveries and investigations that UVEX will be involved with. Perhaps even more exciting, however, are the unexpected elements of the universe it will uncover.

"Every time you look at the skies in a new wavelength, you learn something new and unexpected," El-Badry said.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#766. Malaysian War Drama ‘The Ghost and the Gun’ Sets Global Netflix Release (EXCLUSIVE)

Netflix will stream “The Ghost and the Gun” (“Peluru Senja“), a Bahasa Malaysia-language war drama set in Malaya in the years after World War II, around the world.

The film is the third feature from Indian filmmaker Anshul Tiwari, who is based in Singapore and previously directed “Before Life After Death” and “Bayaar.” Abhi Kumar wrote the screenplay.

The story unfolds in 1948. When British forces pull out of Malaya, two soldiers are left behind – one Malay, one British. The pair have to come to terms with their pasts in the war while defending a village targeted by armed rebels. Related Stories Sofia Franklyn on 'Call Her Daddy,' Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: 'I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I'm Good' Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, Unwell Sign With CAA

“While movies have explored World War II from every Western angle, the human cost paid across Malaya and Singapore remains largely unseen,” Tiwari said. “I was drawn to this story because the volatility of the Malayan Emergency feels painfully urgent today: the timeless tragedy of ordinary people caught in the crossfire of empires fighting for power.”

Malaysian actor Fabian Loo, an award winner known for “Rain Town” and “One Cent Thief,” heads the ensemble. He is joined by Hazman Al-Idrus, Asmara Abigail (“Impetigore,” “Stone Turtle”) and American actor Brett Tutor (“Monsters of Man”).

“Siti carries the weight of a whole region’s history in a very quiet way, and playing her in the Pahang dialect pushed me somewhere new,” Abigail said of her character. “I’m proud that such a Southeast Asian story can now reach audiences everywhere.”

The producers planned the film as an international collaboration from day one. Shooting took place at Viking Sunset Studios in Bali, where 14 sets were built to stand in for 1940s Malaya. The cinematographer came from India, a Malaysian team in Kuala Lumpur handled all of the film’s sound and color work, and a British composer wrote the score. Cast and crew members hailed from Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, India, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S.

“Bringing seven countries together on one production was never the easy route, but it was the right one,” said producer Debasmita Dasgupta of FilmsPositive. “Every department brought something of their own film culture to create a deeply rooted Southeast Asian story. What you see on screen is the result of seamless cross-border collaboration, proof that authentic regional stories have the power to command a global stage.”

Fellow producer Mikail Chowdhury of LDNO said films like this one rarely get made. “A Malay soldier in 1948 Malaya isn’t the story a traditional studio would back, but it’s one which audiences in this region have been waiting to see on screen and should be told,” Chowdhury said. “Independent film is where these stories survive and it is a privilege to have been part of it.”

Dasgupta and Chowdhury produce alongside Tim Willrich of Limbo Pictures and Bo H. Holmgreen, CEO of Viking Sunset Studios. Jessie White of Misfit Studios is executive producer with Mohsen Ashraf of Friendly Felix Studios, Tanveer Ali, Amreen Bashir of Amra Bangladeshi and Tahmid Khan of Auras.

White said Misfit enjoys supporting people who take creative chances on stories they believe in. “We’re proud to have helped make this film happen, and excited for audiences to discover it on Netflix,” White said.

After a nationwide cinema release in Malaysia and a smaller theatrical run in Indonesia, “The Ghost and the Gun” will launch on Netflix worldwide on Nov. 28.

#764. Latin Grammys 2026: Rosalía Wins Album of the Year

Janet Jackson also presented Daddy Yankee with the person of the year honor.

Spanish singer Rosalía took home the top prize of album of the year at the 2026 Latin Grammys on Thursday night for her 2025 album Lux.

She opened the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards, live from Sin City, with an emotive medley of her Lux tracks “La Rumba Del Perdón,” “La Perla” and “Dios Es Un Stalker,” joined by angelic dancers ornamented with halos atop a stage meant to look like heavenly clouds.

It was a reminder of the expansiveness of her album: an offbeat, full-hearted embrace of her classical training through huge orchestral movements, inspired by the lives of female saints. Related Stories TV How to Stream the 2026 Latin Grammys Online Movies 'Wet,' Starring Connor Storrie, Rebecca Ferguson and Odessa A'zion, Acquired by Lionsgate

Her “La Perla” also won song of the year, and during her speech, she thanked Mexico and invited her collaborators on the song, the American urban sierreño trio Yahritza Y Su Esencia, to join her on stage.

Daddy Yankee, the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards’ person of the year and first Latin urbano artist to receive the honor, ripped through his biggest hits an hour into Thursday’s award show, treating the stage like a stadium floor.

It was one for the history books: There were outfit changes, set changes and his native Puerto Rico always at the forefront as he ran through “Ella Me Levantó,” “Con Calma,” “BOTZ,” “Despacito,” “Lo Que Pasó, Pasó,” “Sonríele,” “Rompe,” “Pokito” and, of course, “Gasolina” — joined by Bizarrap, Bad Gyal, Feid, Jay Wheeler, French Montana, LL Cool J and Diljit Dosanjh.

When it came time for Daddy Yankee to receive his honor, it was delivered to him by Janet Jackson “with admiration and respect,” as she said in her speech. When he accepted the award, he concluded by saying “Puerto Rico, recuerda. … Puerto Rico no es pequeño. Pequeño el mapa.” In English: “Puerto Rico, remember. … Puerto Rico is not small. The map is small.”

The award show took place live from Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena. It aired live on Univision, UniMás, Galavisión and ViX and hosted by actor, producer and musician Roselyn Sánchez.

For the first award of the night, Pablo Alboran and Backstreet Boys’ Howie D presented Juanes with best pop/rock album for Juanesteban.

Performances were at a high level: Karol G was joined by a full orchestra and 12 Mariachis for her música mexicana ballad “Ese Hombre es Malo.” Mon Laferte broke hearts with her soulful “Femme Fatale.” Silvana Estrada’s “Dime” bridged culture and heritage with her signature Venezuelan cuatro, a four-stringed instrument similar in structure to a ukulele.

Kany García stunned with her acoustic, aflamencado single “La Niña Que Fui.” The Uruguayan-born Jorge Drexler’s rendition of “Las Palabras” felt like theater. And Argentine rapper Milo J performed “Solifican12” and “Gil,” joined by the Latin American folk icon Gustavo Santaolalla.

Carín León brought the house down with “Desde Que Te Tengo,” as did Juanes and Vivir Quintana with “Humano.” Elena Rose was joined by sword-wielding dancers for “Alma.”

Brazilian superstar Anitta did a medley of her “Equilibrium” hits — “Desgraça,” “Choka Choka” and “Meia Noite” among them — an eclectic mix of Brazilian funk, samba, bossa nova, semba, reggae, electronic pop performed in Portuguese, Spanish and English.

Soon after, she was back on stage accepting the trophy for Portuguese language contemporary pop album. She used her speech to shine a light on the Black culture of her native Brazil.

There was a touching tribute to the late ranchera icon, Mexican singer-songwriter José Alfredo Jiménez, produced by Edgar Barrera: The Warning covered “Te Solté la Rienda,” Reik did “La Media Vuelta,” Sofía Reyes and Yami Safdie dueted “Si Nos Dejan” and Camila Fernández brought it home with a big belting “El Rey.” Not soon afterward, she headed back to the stage to perform a full-throated “Serpiente De Cascabel.”

It was the first of two tributes: The second was for Willie Colón, the social activist and Grammy-nominated architect of urban salsa music, who died in February of this year. His son, Miguel Colón, as well as Nathy Peluso and Luis Figueroa and others performed.

Awards were handed out quickly, too. Karol G took home the trophy for urban music album for Tropicoqueta. Xavi won contemporary Mexican album for Dosis, his first Latin Grammy. Fonseca was presented the trophy for contemporary tropical album shortly thereafter for his album, Antes Que El Tiempo Se Vaya.

Best new artist went to Colombian singer Aria Vega, who gave her acceptance speech through tears. This year, the Latin Recording Academy made changes to the category so that only artists with fewer than three albums or 25 singles released were eligible to win.

Most of the evening’s awards were handed out during a pre-televised Premiere Ceremony. That included Bobby Pulido winning the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album for his release Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol. 2/En Vivo). Just days earlier, Pulido made history in the U.S. midterm elections by securing a seat in the House of Representatives for the Democrats by flipping a Texas district seat.

“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” he said in his acceptance speech.

This dazzling collection of ancient stars could hold clues to the Milky Way's past.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange.

But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed.

The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus.

M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity.

Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old!

Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell.

Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history.

Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

In the story, teenage Johanna dreams of a glittering Twilight vampire prince. Instead, she gets Martti: a balding, beer-bellied 49-year-old bloodsucker who slips into a Santa suit to gain entry to homes and devour entire families. Soon, she finds herself trapped in a bloody and horrific nightmare of ageing masculine toxicity, family trauma, and festive slaughter. Related Stories Sofia Franklyn on 'Call Her Daddy,' Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: 'I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I'm Good' Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, Unwell Sign With CAA

Sold by Charades and produced by Bufo, Allfilm and Hobab, “Red Snow” debuts exclusive clip here:

Mixing vampire mythology with Santa Claus – “and the sexual undertones that come with it” – has surprised some viewers, admitted Rautsi.

“It can be disturbing to people, but it’s not a disturbing film. It’s set in this absurd, outrageous world that hopefully allows me to get away with it. That’s the part of its charm: the grotesque and all the twists and turns in the story.”

After Fantastic Fest and Sitges, “Red Snow” is now heading to Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival and has been at the AFM. Hannu-Pekka Björkman, Anni Iikkanen, Tommi Korpela, Kari Hietalahti and Marja-Liisa Nguyen star.

It was important to still ground the film in some “recognizable emotion,” stated Rautsi.

“These are heightened characters, but there are also some glimmers of what they are actually going through. We don’t necessarily have to root for them all the time, but we’re along for the ride – despite all the madness.”

Christmas can be a stressful time, with or without vampires.

“For me, this juicy Christmas setting acts as a boiling kettle. We’ve all been there. We know the feeling of spending Christmas with family when you’re supposed to be jolly but it’s actually miserable,” he laughed.

“You can see this in all of Shane Black’s films that are set at Christmas but not about Christmas. I think they have affected me, too.”

Rautsi doesn’t hide his affection for horror. Known for shorts “Helsinki Mansplaining Massacre” and “The Night of the Living Dicks,” he has also written “Nightborn” and “Hatching.”

“I’m a nervous person. A good horror film is my comfort zone, though, because it validates the internal life of someone who’s afraid. Fear is such a taboo subject – people don’t talk about it. But then we go and see a horror film, and we celebrate the fact that it’s O.K. to be afraid. It can be fun to experience it in a safe setting,” he said.

Despite its wild premise, “Red Snow” captures how he perceives life. It can be scary, but it can also make you laugh.

“I’m constantly laughing about all the things I’m afraid of. The goal of the film was to express how I experience things. You can be going through something ridiculous and then notice something beautiful about the whole situation. Life can be so many things, all at once, within the space of five seconds.”

#760. How London-Based Facialist Keren Bartov Prepped Hollywood for This Fall’s Starriest Soirees

Cate Blanchett, Mikey Madison and Elizabeth Debicki made a pit stop at the aesthetician’s Notting Hill clinic ahead of the Harper’s Bazaar Women of the Year Awards.

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, The Hollywood Reporter may receive an affiliate commission.

Lightyears before Hollywood’s obsession with beauty biohacking, Keren Bartov was already using medical-grade, high-tech skin care tools to bring glow-from-within radiance to stars’ visages. Her results were most recently seen on clients Cate Blanchett, Elizabeth Debicki and Mikey Madison, who visited the celebrity facialist’s Notting Hill studio for bespoke facials ahead of the annual Harper’s Bazaar Women of the Year Awards in London on Nov. 5.

The 47-year-old aesthetician also saved A-listers from a cross-Atlantic trip by popping up in LA with her suite of skin-plumping, jawline-snatching devices and her own Keren Bartov Advanced Skin Care serums and creams ahead of the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show and Academy Museum Gala last month. VS Angels models Joan Smalls, Jasmine Tookes, Elsa Hosk and Amelia Gray beamed with Bartov’s signature glow at the lingerie company’s takeover of Sony Pictures Studios on Oct. 18, as did longtime clients Demi Moore and Mila Kunis at the star-studded Academy fundraiser. She also prepped Kim Kardashian’s skin for her 46th birthday party, and also works with Beyonce and mom Tina Knowles, Julia Roberts, Michelle Monaghan, Eiza Gonzalez, Anya Taylor-Joy and Olivia Wilde, to name just a handful. Related Stories Lifestyle Our Top 29 Holiday Gifts of 2026 Lifestyle The Top 23 Holiday Gifts for Movie Lovers, From Retro Collectibles to Modern Tech

“Before a major event, my goal is for the skin to look its absolute best while remaining calm, balanced and refreshed. The last thing I want is to cause irritation or an unexpected reaction right before a red carpet,” notes Bartov. “I often combine technologies that help improve the appearance of firmness and texture with lymphatic drainage, gentle enzymatic exfoliation and skin care that delivers hydration and radiance.”

In fact, the U.K.-based skin expert has an arsenal of more than 50 technologies — in which she’s invested millions of dollars to ensure only the most state-of-the-art facials — “but the number itself isn’t what matters. It’s knowing when to use each one, in what order and in what combination,” explains Bartov. “I’m always looking for [products] that allow me to achieve more precise results with less aggressive intervention. I never introduce a technology or ingredient simply because it’s new or everyone is talking about it. For me, innovation has to be backed by science, safety and meaningful results.”

Her pre-event treatments are based on her 90-minute Signature Glow Facial ($500 to $900), available at her London and Tel Aviv clinics. She incorporates her namesake luxury skin-care products along with the Onda Pro (which uses microwave and cool waves to tighten, contour and reduce cellulite), the Lumenis TriLift (which incorporates radiofrequency, microneedling and muscle stimulation for firming and lifting), the buzzy XERF (Bartov was among the first to add the radiofrequency skin-tightening machine to her menu) and other non-invasive, multi-modality medical devices.

For the Victoria’s Secret and Academy events, “I treated clients with completely different skin concerns, which meant every protocol was different. What they all had in common was the desire for skin that looked naturally healthy, fresh, and radiant, creating the perfect canvas for makeup without ever looking overdone,” says Bartov.

A former aspiring actor, Bartov’s unexpected path to Hollywood began in southern Israel, where she opened a tiny skin clinic in her community before expanding to Tel Aviv. Fellow Israeli Gal Gadot became her first celebrity client and earliest cheerleader, and pushed Bartov to bring her methodology to London in 2023.

Bartov recently debuted a Festive Facial to prep clients’ faces for upcoming holiday soirees. Like her signature offering, the clinical treatment uses up to five tech tools in a specific sequence to address collagen loss, pigmentation, acne and signs of aging. Visitors can also pick up her limited-edition holiday gift sets (from $400) created in collaboration with British artist Clym Evernden, who also drew up a winter window dressing for Bartov’s Notting Hill clinic.

Can’t book a flight or secure an appointment at her overseas outposts? Bartov’s skin-care sets are also available online for anyone to achieve her red carpet-ready glow from home.

Ahead, Bartov shares what she can’t live without (including her most priceless essentials), the ingredients and devices that have piqued her interest and those that she recommends skipping.

In a nutshell, what led you to becoming a star-trusted skin expert?

Keren Bartov: Ever since I was a little girl, I’ve been drawn to everything related to beauty, aesthetics and skin care. It was always something I loved, but as I got older, I realized I also wanted a stable career, something I could build and grow over time, so I decided to study cosmetology. Very quickly, I discovered there was so much more to it than I had imagined. I fell in love with the field, started studying and exploring it in depth and realized I had found my place.

Today, I feel like I’ve somehow managed to bring all the worlds I love together: beauty, aesthetics, creativity, working with people and even a little bit of the entertainment world, especially when I’m preparing actresses and models for some of their biggest moments.

For more than 17 years, I’ve been studying, researching and exploring advanced technologies and treatment methods from around the world. What started as genuine curiosity and passion eventually became the treatment method I’ve developed over the years.

Developing my own skin-care line was a natural extension of that journey. I wanted to take the knowledge and experience I’d gained in the treatment room and translate it into products that could become part of my clients’ everyday routines. To this day, nothing excites me more than seeing how the right treatment and skin-care routine can transform not only someone’s skin, but also their confidence.

How do you decide what new product or technology makes the cut? What are the red flags that tell you something is just a fad?

I never introduce a technology or ingredient simply because it’s new or everyone is talking about it. For me, innovation has to be backed by science, safety and meaningful results.

Before incorporating a new device or product, I look at the research behind it, how it works, whether it’s suitable for different skin types and how it can complement the treatments and products I already use.

I take exactly the same approach when developing my own skin care. Every formula needs to have a clear purpose. For example, with Melanin Correcting Serum, the focus is on addressing the appearance of uneven pigmentation, while Hydra Reboost Cream is about providing the hydration and comfort the skin needs. They’re different products designed to address different concerns, and that’s exactly how I believe skin care should work.

What ingredients, devices, or innovations are exciting you most right now, and why?

One technology I’m particularly excited about is Onda Pro, which uses targeted microwave energy to address concerns including skin firmness and the appearance of facial contours. What interests me most is how I can incorporate it into a broader, personalized treatment protocol.

Another is XERF, a radiofrequency technology designed for non-invasive skin tightening. I was among the first practitioners in the world to work with it, and I love being involved in the early stages of exploring new technologies, understanding their capabilities and discovering who can truly benefit from them.

When it comes to ingredients, I’m a strong believer in peptides, active acids, and ingredients supported by solid clinical research. I’m not interested in whatever ingredient happens to be trending online. I’m interested in what can genuinely address a specific skin concern.

Peptides are particularly interesting to me, which is why I love incorporating a peptide serum into a targeted skin-care routine. I’m also a big believer in exfoliating acids when they’re used correctly. My Booster Peel & Glow Serum reflects that approach: using active ingredients with a clear purpose, rather than exfoliating simply for the sake of it.

To me, real innovation isn’t always about discovering something entirely new. It’s about finding smarter, more precise ways to use ingredients and technologies that have already proven themselves.

What beauty trends do you suggest clients skip?

I’m not a big fan of beauty gimmicks that look amazing on social media but don’t necessarily deliver meaningful, long-term results.

Sheet masks and under-eye patches are good examples. They can provide a temporary boost of hydration or make the skin feel refreshed, but I don’t see them as a substitute for skin care that genuinely works on the skin.

I’d much rather see someone invest in a well-formulated serum that addresses their actual skin concerns. That’s why I’ve always placed so much emphasis on active formulas, whether it’s Advanced Skin Serum as part of a consistent routine or Melanin Correcting Serum for someone looking to address uneven skin tone.

I’m also cautious about trends like at-home microneedling. It’s a procedure that requires professional knowledge, and when done incorrectly, it can cause irritation, infection and damage to the skin. Another trend I’m not a fan of is using active acids without understanding their concentrations, how they interact, or whether they’re suitable for your skin.

I absolutely believe in advanced skin care and using multiple products, but every product should have a purpose. I don’t believe in adding something to your routine just because it’s gone viral. For me, the question isn’t how good a product looks on camera. It’s what it actually does for your skin.

Walk us through your treatments. What do you consider when creating custom protocols for clients?

No two people have exactly the same skin, so no two treatments should ever be identical. I start with a thorough skin assessment, looking at texture, hydration levels, pigmentation, elasticity and sensitivity. I also consider age, lifestyle, skin-care habits, previous treatments and, of course, what the client wants to achieve.

One of the things that makes my method different is the ability to address several concerns within a single treatment. For example, I might combine technologies targeting firmness, texture, hydration, and radiance, carefully selecting devices that complement one another. But personalization doesn’t end when the client leaves the clinic. I also look at what they’re using at home, because professional treatments and daily skin care should support one another.

Someone dealing with pigmentation might benefit from incorporating Melanin Correcting Serum into their routine, while someone whose skin needs more hydration might be better suited to Hydra Reboost Cream. In other cases, I might focus on introducing active serums gradually or adjusting the evening routine.

I don’t believe in a one-size-fits-all facial or a one-size-fits-all skin-care routine. I believe in understanding exactly what the skin needs and building the right protocol around it.

What are your top tips for a solid foundational skin-care routine? What people avoid?

I’m a big believer in a comprehensive skin-care routine that incorporates multiple products and active ingredients, as long as they’re carefully selected and work well together. I don’t think we should be afraid of having several steps. What’s important is understanding what each product does and why it’s there.

For me, the foundation of great skin is proper cleansing, targeted active ingredients, hydration, and daily sun protection.

In the evening, I always recommend starting with a double cleanse. I use my Micellar Water to remove makeup and impurities, followed by a gentle milky cleanser to thoroughly cleanse the skin.

Once the skin is clean, I like to work with different serums depending on its needs. Booster Peel & Glow Serum is one of my favorites for improving the appearance of skin texture and radiance, while Advanced Skin Serum is an essential part of my own routine.

For clients dealing with uneven skin tone and pigmentation, I often recommend Melanin Correcting Serum. I also love incorporating a peptide serum, as peptides are among the ingredients I believe in for supporting firmer, healthier-looking skin.

I place enormous importance on nighttime skin care. While we sleep, the skin goes through natural renewal and repair processes, and I love using those hours to give it targeted care.

One ingredient I believe in most is retinol. It’s one of the most extensively researched ingredients in skin care, with well-established benefits for improving skin texture, the appearance of fine lines, and uneven skin tone over time.

That belief was also behind the development of Next Gen, my retinol-infused night cream. I consider it an important part of a targeted evening routine, with the frequency of use adjusted to the individual’s skin.

Hydration is equally important. I love Hydra Reboost Cream for keeping the skin feeling comfortable and moisturized, and Hydration Glow Spray is one of my favorite finishing touches for an instant boost of freshness and radiance. It’s also a product I love having with me when I travel.

In the morning, my focus is on hydration, protection and maintaining healthy-looking skin. Sunscreen is absolutely non-negotiable.

Of course, not every active ingredient is suitable for everyone, and I don’t recommend layering strong acids and retinol indiscriminately. It’s important to tailor combinations and frequency of use to the skin’s needs and tolerance.

What should we avoid? Constantly switching products, combining active ingredients without understanding how they work together and expecting overnight results.

I always compare skin care to going to the gym. If you want to see real results, you have to be consistent. It’s the combination of the right products, a consistent routine and professional treatments that makes the difference.

What are some essentials that you can’t live without right now?

If there’s one skin-care product I can’t live without, it’s my Advanced Skin Serum. It’s one of the products I reach for every single day and a true essential in my routine. I love how it helps my skin look smoother, fresher and more radiant. No matter where I’m traveling, it always comes with me.

I’m a big believer in movement and taking care of my body. Strength training is an important part of my routine, and I also love going for walks. With all the traveling and work, it’s my time to clear my head and focus on myself.

I love activewear that’s comfortable enough for a workout but stylish enough to wear outside the gym. Alo Yoga’s Airlift leggings are exactly my style, especially on days when I’m going straight from a workout to meetings or errands.

I absolutely love Victoria Beckham’s tailoring. There’s something so precise, feminine and effortlessly elegant about her designs. A beautifully tailored blazer and trousers are a combination I can always rely on, especially for meetings and events.

I love this bag. There’s something iconic and timeless about it, and I’ve always preferred pieces that never go out of style.

For me, great foundation should still let your skin look like skin. I love a lightweight base that evens out the complexion, adds freshness and lets the skin’s natural texture show through. That’s exactly the kind of makeup I gravitate toward.

I love makeup that adds a subtle touch of light without looking heavy. This is one of those products that can instantly bring a little color and radiance to the face, especially when I’m going straight from a long workday to dinner or an event.

I love candles and beautiful home fragrances, and Diptyque is one of my favorite brands. Baies has that elegant, comforting scent that instantly creates a lovely atmosphere at home. Lighting a candle at the end of the day is one of my little rituals.

And one thing I could never leave off the list: Evenings at Home With My Husband and Kids.

This might not be a product, but it’s the one thing I truly can’t live without. I spend so much time traveling and working around the world that the simplest moments at home mean the most to me. Family dinners, spending time with my kids or just having a quiet evening with my husband are the moments I look forward to most.

"The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground.

Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027.

"Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher."

Rocket Lab is best known for Electron, a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO).

Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO.

Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control).

Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30.

The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s.

"The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said.

That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket. For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. The rocket has a reusable first stage and can carry about 25 tons (22.7 metric tons) to LEO.

The medium lifter has been the world's most prolific rocket for the past few years. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number of orbital missions as all other launchers in the world combined. And all 165 of those flights were successful.

But SpaceX is phasing out the Falcon 9 — and its heavy-lift cousin, the Falcon Heavy — nonetheless, shifting all launch work over to its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which can haul more than 100 tons to LEO.

There's a real worry among folks in the space community that this massive payload capacity won't be available to them for a while. SpaceX has made it pretty clear that early Starship operations will be geared toward internal priorities — specifically, the buildout of SpaceX's Starlink V3 broadband network and its Starmind AI data-center constellation.

These will be very big jobs, even for the most powerful rocket ever built. For example, the Starlink V3 megaconstellation will consist of about 100,000 satellites, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk. Starship can carry about 60 of these spacecraft to LEO per launch, so just building out the constellation will require about 1,700 liftoffs.

The numbers for Starmind will be even more mind-boggling, for SpaceX wants that constellation to eventually harbor a million satellites.

The coming launch bottleneck should increase demand for Electron as well as Neutron, Beck said during Monday's call. After all, many small-satellite operators have launched with SpaceX over the years, booking spots on Falcon 9 "rideshare" flights. And those opportunities are now drying up.

"The next logical alternative is of course an Electron, so we see tremendous traction there," Beck said.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#756. ‘Pop Pop’ Dives Into Radicalization and Male Fragility in the Digital Age. Its Creator Says It’s “More Topical Every Day” – and Urges Us to Join Hands.

Writer-director Dylan Stephen Levers' debut feature is a cinematic parable, premiering at Tallinn, that was partly shot at alt-right marches and is full of memes and indie spirit.

U.S. filmmaker Dylan Stephen Levers’ (this is a film about tom and maddy) debut feature, Pop Pop, is a cinematic parable that hits us not only with unusual and memorable visuals and sounds, but also hits us hard with all sorts of queasiness-inducing questions for our age of virality, digital nihilism, the manosphere and radicalization.

In true independent spirit and pop art fashion, the movie is a cinematic mash-up of meme culture, trips into cyberspace and alt-right protests that explores toxic masculinity, cancel culture and a sea of identity crises without any apparent lifeboats. Related Stories TV "Evil All Along": How Russell Brand Got Caught Business Around 10-15 Percent of SAG-AFTRA Membership Wants AI Blocked, CEO Tells Web Summit

Pop Pop gets its world premiere on Sunday, Nov. 15 during the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia. And it only seems fitting that it debuts in the fest’s Rebels With a Cause Competition program.

Written and directed by Levers, Pop Pop stars Cashton Tate Rehklau, Trevor Jonathan Lown and Lena Kutscher, along with Austin Davis, Djuna Knight, Kevin Confoy and Marta Kotzien. Rehklau and Lown are Dustin and Dibz, best friends who survived their senior year of college and now share an apartment in New York and an Internet series. But where do they go from here? Well, they end up taking very different paths.

Dustin becomes immersed in an increasingly radical worldview, focusing on attracting attention and a following via provocative online posts. Dibz finds meaning in social justice activism and his first crush on a man, forcing him to reconsider his identity. The film mixes fictional scenes with footage shot during real-life protests and psychedelic animations that take the audience into the digital world, including the manosphere.

Pop Pop is a Body by Lulz Films production, co-produced by Grease NYC. The cinematographer is Consuelo Althouse, while Josh Coll handled editing. W. Ian Ross, Levers and Althouse produced Pop Pop, with Stefanie Abel Horowitz, Josh Bierne-Golden and Erin Magill serving as executive producers.

In a director’s statement, Levers says he began writing Pop Pop in 2016, “as angry white men were gathering online, sharing extremist ideas about immigrants, Islam, women, and the supposed destruction of the ‘white race.’ What the media dismissed as a fringe movement soon became a significant political force.”

The filmmaker decided to explore what it means to be a man today. Ahead of its world premiere, Levers talked to THR about Pop Pop, his inspirations and hopes for the film, and how the U.S., and the world, may be able to be less divided – or at least divided with less rage.

When and how did the inspiration to create Pop Pop hit you?

I started writing this many, many years ago. The coming-of-age tale is evergreen in film and TV. Especially in the U.S., there were things coming out like Girls and Frances Ha that so many of my friends were really identifying with because they talked very eloquently about young womanhood and graduating from being a girl to an adult. But I thought, “Well, where’s the conversation around men?” I started convening groups of people for little sessions and just writing things here and there. I come from a theater background, so this was developed like a new play. We would get together every six months with a group of actors and just hammer away at the script and make it better and better. In February of 2020, it felt ready to go. And three weeks later, there was COVID, and the world shut down.

It felt a little dead on arrival. But throughout that summer of 2020, a lot of the things that were already present as narrative came to the forefront even more. The film is set in the middle of the 2016 election cycle, but issues around masculinity, what it means to be a man, what it means to be in community with other people, whether that’s digital or otherwise, almost felt like they were on steroids now. It’s become, strangely, more and more topical every day.

Since you mentioned the election that first made Donald Trump U.S. President, I want to ask you about political marches that we see in Pop Pop. It looks like you actually shot during real protests…did you?

I had done all this research in 2019 about these alt-right protests, and I had been to a bunch of them. Famously, there was one in the Boston area called the “Straight Pride” protest, and the parade marshal was Milo Yiannopoulos. It felt very fringe and very contained, but if you were there, you felt, “Oh my god, we can’t turn away. This is just going to get bigger and bigger.”

And the filmmaker part of me felt it just saw such amazing production value in this horrible protest. So, how do we recreate that on screen? And our cinematographer, Consuelo Althouse, because she’s a genius and has an amazing background in doc filmmaking, said one of the things that we could do was shoot in some of these protests. So we did.

[A consultant on the political things on the film] told us that the protest that we really should be going to was in D.C., which was a “Stop the Steal” protest led by this guy Ali Alexander. It ended up being in December of 2020, three weeks before Jan. 6. And so it ultimately functioned as the dress rehearsal for Jan. 6. And as we were watching the news that day, we were like, “Oh my God, that guy’s in our footage! That guy’s in the footage! And that guy!”

How did you approach or think about filming inside those protests, especially sending in your actor who plays Dibz?

Consuelo and I had a lot of conversations about the ethics of shooting in an event that had its own purpose and was not being staged for the purpose of being on screen. We made a pact to take this one character, Dibz, and let the action unfold around him. We were not going to try to affect any part of the proceedings of that day, but let’s try to see if we can really catch those colors, those textures, the craziness of the day, which, even if we had millions of dollars for production design, would not have looked as authentic as what you see on screen

Trevor, who plays Dibz, is such an amazing and brave actor. But it was definitely always safety first. In no way was I willing to traumatize any crew or cast members by making this film, and in no way were we trying to put anybody’s lives in physical danger. We said if anything sketchy happens, we’d regroup at a meeting point. So we had precautions in place. There were a couple of people, as we were shooting throughout the day, who were like, “Why do you have such a large camera? What are you guys doing?” And we just said, “Oh, we’re an independent outlet,” and they loved the idea that we weren’t the corporate media.

In Pop Pop, we see some modern-looking scenes in the cyber sphere but also an older-looking computer with its loud typing sounds and retro-feeling pop-up windows and the like. Can you explain how important it was for you that the technology side of the story of the film was reflected by the visual experience?

I always love to ask what the organizing principle of a story is. I thought of this computer screen almost as a character to start priming the audience for the rules of that kind of existence. The idea was to put this device into this story that’s a deeply digital one.

And the digital space is a mix of stuff that we made up and actual memes. There are memes that would have been popular in 2016. There’s a Drake dancing, there’s Obama, they’re flying over what’s called the political compass, which is a meme that lets you self-locate where you are politically, and then there are some more obscure gems. My biggest dream for this movie is, and I’ll know I have made it then, that somebody writes a listicle called “25 Memes That You Can See in Pop Pop.”

Since you just mentioned the title again, how did you choose that?

To me, it was about the feeling of everything breaking apart. My generation in the States grew up with this idea that institutions were healthy and that there were certain social contracts that would never be broken. But we have seen in the past 12-plus years that there’s been a giant pickaxe that has been taken to that version of reality. So, the title is in reference to that breaking down and that combustible tinderbox energy of everything just sort of blowing up.

But it is also that this is pop filmmaking, which is about swallowing everything and metabolizing it so it becomes this different thing. Here’s all this imagery – let’s put it through the wringer and talk about it, interrogate it, and see where we land. So it’s a little bit of an accidental double entendre.

You say double entendre, so I need to ask you about that great double act that your two leads are. And Lena and the others give it all a real ensemble vibe.These brilliant young actors are giving incredible performances. I cannot wait for people to see them. They are amazing. I really hope that we can introduce people to them. I am so excited for people to see them for the first time.

I assume you didn’t have a huge budget and didn’t win the lottery?

No, I worked to pay the bills and keep the lights on, producing big events for brands [and things like that as a day job]. I just kept Tetris-ing every single job I possibly could into my schedule without going absolutely insane. I was doing crazy shit, including following a giant Bath & Body Works candle around the Eastern Seaboard or going to the Grove in L.A. telling people to use circular Legos, not the square ones. I also got really lucky in that my collaborators were really down and kept coming back to this project time and time again.

I think this was true indie filmmaking. The hope and dream is that, as we watch in our industry all of these conglomerates sell to each other and combine forces, what happens is a healthier indie undercurrent, so that films like this and filmmakers who have ideas that are a little bit more out there can get their films made with less strife than five years of Tetris-ing so many jobs together.

In the “thank you” section of the credits, I saw the name Zazie Beetz. Is that THE Zazie Beetz?

Yes, she and her now-husband David [Rysdahl] did some very early development on this film.

After I watched Pop Pop, I felt motivated to try harder again to keep in dialogue with people who may not always share my political or other ideas or hopes. What’s your hope for audiences of Pop Pop?

I hope it causes massive fights and wrecks entire families. No, I’m kidding! (laughs) I really set out to make a movie about people who are right when they’re wrong and wrong when they’re right and what it means to be morally three-dimensional in a world that provides us with not many great options for being a good person.

So, yes, I wanted to ask how we deal with other people who we potentially don’t agree with, but we still have to be in community with. It’s really about thinking seriously about community building and coalition building. I think one of the things that this country has to do is to figure out how we can build coalitions, and part of that is joining hands with people that we don’t necessarily always agree with and figuring out what is still left in the concentric circles between us.

It’s my hope that folks can utilize the film as a jumping-off point to talk about their own struggles. A lot of us are about to go home for Thanksgiving and have anxiety-inducing political conversations around the family table. Perhaps, once you see this movie, instead of pointing to your uncle with whom you disagree, or fighting with your mother, you can look at these characters and use them as ciphers to have discussions instead of pointing fingers.

I’m hungry for other filmmakers to go out there and make films that really are responding to and rising to meet the moment, and I want to meet them.

#755. Aly Muritiba Says It Was ‘Revolutionary’ to Centre Black Joy in Brazilian Musical ‘Funk’ Led by Rising Star Duda Santos

The film is playing in competition at the Huelva Ibero-American Film Festival

At first glance, it might seem as if Aly Muritiba took quite a sharp turn with “Funk,” the high-octane musical that follows the Venice-selected “Private Desert” and Gramado closer “Drenched in Blood.” But a closer look reveals how all three films, as well as many of the director’s other lauded works, are informed by a curiosity around loneliness and desire. In “Funk,” that curiosity lends itself to the portrayal of a young woman whose life’s dream is to become a Brazilian funk star, but whose journey to the top comes with great personal sacrifice. Related Stories Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, Unwell Sign With CAA Sofia Franklyn on 'Call Her Daddy,' Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: 'I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I'm Good'

Playing in competition at the Huelva Ibero-American Film Festival, “Funk” premiered in Tribeca and kicks off with a burst of energy at a party in a favela in Rio de Janeiro. That is where Sabrina (Duda Santos) feels her best, stepping onto the stage and into her MC persona to sing about explicit sexual desires to the bass-heavy beats of funk, the Brazilian rhythm that won the hearts of major international stars like Madonna and The Weeknd. Sabrina is a rocket, a determined young woman who dreams of making it big and is unapologetic about her desires—both professional and sexual.

Speaking with Variety ahead of Huelva, Muritiba says the idea to “speak about favela from a different perspective” came from producers Heitor Dhalia and Manoel Rangel. Both had shot series in the favelas of Rio de Janeiro and had witnessed the “potency of funk.” The duo then invited the director into the project, with the newly-formed trio brainstorming the character of Sabrina.

Muritiba’s research process was “empirical,” with the director attending several different funk parties across Rio while working on the script and the visual concept for the film. Casting came soon after, with “Funk” boasting a large ensemble cast including several real-life funk singers like Lellê and MC Nem.

“Casting was conducted by the very talented Alonso Zerbinato, who cast from the favelas and funk parties across Rio,” says Muritiba. “The majority of the ensemble consists of real-life funk singers, but I needed an experienced actress for the main role because Sabrina is a very complex character.”

The answer for Sabrina came in the shape of Duda Santos, whose burgeoning career has skyrocketed in the last two years thanks to main roles in massively popular telenovelas such as “Garota do Momento” and “A Nobreza do Amor.” “Duda is a great actress, but also a great dancer,” noted the director. “After several roles on TV, she was anxious for her first film role, so she grabbed this opportunity with open arms.”

“Duda is a very serious and hard-working professional,” he adds. “For ‘Funk,’ she had to undergo hours of preparation every day, take singing, dancing, and stage presence lessons on top of extended rehearsals for all scenes. It’s very gratifying to see such a young actress be this talented and committed to her craft.”

Despite having broken out internationally and being appropriated by English-and Spanish-language singers, Brazilian funk has long been stigmatized due to its sexual content and its roots in the lower-class favelas, a contradiction that furthers an idea of Latin American art being valued when regurgitated by Americans and Europeans while homegrown artists are shunned and overlooked. Muritiba was very aware of such stigmas, especially when it comes to the rhythm’s hypersexualization, and decided to face them “without prejudice and conservatism.”

“In the context of the favela, to talk about sex or have sex is to celebrate life and freedom,” he adds. “When you portray and sing about Black bodies living, having fun, having sex and having pleasure in a country with over 300 years of slavery and where high numbers of Black people are murdered every day, is revolutionary.”

Muritiba brings up the fact that Brazil has long had films about favelas celebrated internationally, such as “City of God” and “Elite Squad,” but the subgenre usually portrays Black people through a biased lens involving constant suffering. “What ‘Funk’ proposes is the very opposite: Black people happy, alive, and vibrant. We don’t have a single gunshot in the film. This is revolutionary.”

Music was, of course, key to the success of “Funk.” The film features all original songs, composed by Ambulantes in partnership with DJ Renan Valle. “It was a very rich process creating the songs from the ground up,” says the director. “Choosing the beats and writing the lyrics was great to shape the film’s rhythm.”

The director notes how shooting in the favelas came with its own set of challenges but also great joy. “Going up and down hills, stairs, little streets and seeing the poverty faced by so many Brazilians was very difficult, but it was also beautiful to experience a latent sense of community amongst the locals, something that contaminated the film.”

Muritiba is thrilled to still be showing the film at festivals, but has currently turned his attention to his next film, titled “New Eden.” Starring Welket Bungué, Gabriela Pousa, and Zahy Tentehar, the film follows Damião, a young Black priest who arrives in the titular village in Southern Brazil. For now, all the director can say is that the folk horror will premiere next year at a “major international festival.”

#754. ‘Heartland’ Review: Jessica Chastain Does Sturdy Work as a Hard-Edged Former Country Music Star Saddled With a Thriller in Name Only

Writer-director Shana Feste ('Country Strong') dives into Nashville’s sleazy underbelly in a mystery built on dark secrets, also starring Garrett Hedlund and country singer Carter Faith.

Imagine an episode of ABC’s Nashville written by Taylor Sheridan, but despite a load of fun stuff — a disappearance, a murder plot, festering secrets, shady talent management, an obsessive stalker, a shootout, cowboy boots and Stetsons — it barely has a pulse. Writer-director Shana Feste returns to the milieu of her instantly forgotten 2010 Gwyneth Paltrow vehicle Country Strong, this time going several shades darker. But even after watching the suspense-free Netflix original for two hours, I had to refer to the press notes to learn that it’s a “gritty neo-noir thriller.” Sure, Jan. Related Stories TV 'Below' Star Rohan Campbell on Finding That Newfoundland Accent and Losing Himself in Roles TV Gang Dong-won, Kim Go-eun to Lead Netflix's Period Romance-Action Drama 'The Twilight Between Us'

Jessica Chastain stars as Misty Jones, a country music legend who fled Nashville 20 years earlier, leaving a failed marriage, a career downturn and a lot of bad press behind her. We know she’s been bruised and hardened by experience because she wears no makeup, stringy hair and ratty tank tops, living as a recluse on a remote Georgia pecan farm with her decrepit dogs. She also helpfully pops on a video of an old TV interview at one point, which should be labeled “exposition.” Heartland The Bottom Line Dullsville. Release date: Friday, Nov. 13Cast: Jessica Chastain, Garrett Hedlund, Carter Faith, Ross Lynch, Paul Sparks, Jennifer Nettles, John Hawkes, Hill Harper, Norbert Leo Butz, Wynn EverettDirector-screenwriter: Shana Feste Rated R, 1 hour 53 minutes

Misty interrupts her life of boozing and bar pickups when her brother Donny (Paul Sparks) calls asking for her help following the disappearance of his 22-year-old daughter Charlie Hart (rising country star Carter Faith in a passable acting debut). Charlie has become a significant music figure in a relatively short time, pumping out 10 albums and touring nonstop. Even though she has gone AWOL and resurfaced in the past — showing up late or not at all for concerts and disappointing her fans — Donny is convinced she’s in trouble after being unable to reach her for three days. With his wife undergoing cancer treatment, Donny can’t go to Nashville to look for Charlie, so he convinces her abrasive estranged aunt to go instead.

Even before Misty arrives back in Music City, Donny steers her toward two suspects — Jared Granger (JP Edwards), a sicko stalker whose attentions prompted Charlie to take out a restraining order; and her boyfriend Jace Jacobs (Ross Lynch), a cocky young country rocker whose romantic duets with Charlie tell a different story to their real relationship. Neither Donny nor Misty buys the statement of Charlie’s manager Kelly (Wynn Everett) that she’s merely taking a break on a songwriting retreat.

Frustrated that the cops have turned up nothing, Misty tries putting pressure on them. But her sharp elbows get her stonewalled by Detective White (Norbert Leo Butz), who recalls she was once known as “The Queen of Mean.” “No, it was actually the C**t of Country,” replies Misty, reworking a line that once got Carlene Carter into trouble. Charlie’s history of sudden disappearances means the cops don’t take the case seriously.

Reconnecting with her old musician friend Bucky (Ben Dickey) at a bar, Misty meets record label owner Roy Combs (Garrett Hedlund), who has a reputation for launching new talents at the venue and was the architect of Charlie’s ascendancy. Despite their mutual attraction, Misty keeps Roy at arm’s length in subsequent encounters.

No sooner has Bucky warned her to tread carefully — Nashville has changed and she no longer has the protection of being famous — than Misty gets run off the road by a pickup truck while driving at night. She also comes home to find evidence of an intruder. Only when she goes looking for clues at Charlie’s house, finding blood and signs of a disturbance, then stumbles onto her niece’s bloodied sweats in Granger’s shed does Det. White announce to press that the missing person case has now become an active murder investigation.

By this point, the audience should be pulled into the mystery, especially as secrets come tumbling out, starting with a bombshell Misty drops on a TV talkshow. But Feste’s script lacks the tension or dread to build dramatic momentum, even as new elements come to light and Misty finds herself in serious danger. One problem is that two of the main suspects are too painfully obvious to be guilty, while the real culprit is easy to guess, well before Charlie turns up to provide answers.

Chastain was coached in vocals, piano and guitar for the role, doing all her own singing with assurance. There’s some appeal in watching Misty take over when antagonistic Jace pulls her out on stage during one of his shows or hearing her belt out the title song alongside country royalty Winnie Jo Lean (Jennifer Nettles, bringing strong pipes and folksy sparkle to a two-scene role).

But Chastain was better served by the twangy vocal opportunities of George & Tammy or the Gospel fervor of The Eyes of Tammy Faye, which bagged her a best actress Oscar for one of her least memorable films. There’s a rich history of Hollywood actresses persuasively inhabiting country music stars — Reese Witherspoon in Walk the Line, Sissy Spacek and Beverly D’Angelo in Coal Miner’s Daughter, Karen Black in Altman’s Nashville — but Heartland doesn’t give Chastain anything close to that kind of space to shine. Though she does get to say lines like “I’ma go get my gun.”

Naturally, pretty-voiced Faith also performs her own songs here, as do Lynch as Jace and John Hawkes in a brief appearance as Misty’s ex-husband. The weak link in the cast is Hedlund (reuniting with Feste after Country Strong), who communicates little of Roy’s shifty charisma, beyond the sign stapled to his forehead with the word “corrupt” in bold red letters. More than any actor’s shortcomings, however, the big issue is the director’s tendency to let the film keep going slack when it should be tightening the knot. Unable to foster much emotional investment in its characters, it’s Country Weak.

#752. Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
