With comets out of the picture, attention now turns to asteroids or even Earth itself as the source of prebiotic chemistry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet.

Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth.

Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement.

Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets.For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely.

Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves.

In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS.

The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second).Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke."

It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet.

However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth.

Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA.

However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars, because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity."This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet."

More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1, where all the planets are bunched up close.

In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive.

The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#751. Renny Harlin Launches Harlin House Fellowship for Emerging European Filmmakers, Taps Colin Trevorrow, Tim Miller as Advisors

Finnish director Renny Harlin has set up Harlin House, a production company that will mentor emerging European directors and help them turn their projects into genre features with commercial reach.

Harlin unveiled the venture and its fellowship program on Nov. 13 at Helsinki’s Night Visions International Film Festival.

Filmmakers chosen for the Harlin House Fellowship will develop their projects with Harlin and an advisory board, and the company will pick titles from the program to produce. Harlin House aims to make its first film next year, then scale up to a minimum of two films annually. It is targeting seven to 10 features over its first five years. Related Stories Sofia Franklyn on 'Call Her Daddy,' Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: 'I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I'm Good' Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, Unwell Sign With CAA

Harlin co-founded the company with producer Johanna Harlin, who will run its community and podcast, and Max Michael of M3 Global Strategy.

“I also know what it means to arrive from Europe with a story to tell and no clear path into Hollywood,” Harlin said. “Helping another filmmaker find that path is a central part of this company’s mission.”

The founding advisory board is made up of Colin Trevorrow (“Jurassic World,” “Jurassic World Dominion”), Tim Miller (“Deadpool,” “Terminator: Dark Fate”), “Minions” and “Despicable Me 3” director Kyle Balda and Janet Change Balda. Between them, they cover live action, VFX and animation.

“Fans have been the driving force behind my career. They are the reason these films get made and the reason they continue to find new audiences years later,” Harlin said. “With Harlin House, I want to bring them closer to the process and give them an opportunity to participate in what we build.”

Using the global investment platform Republic Film, fans can come aboard as founding investors and share in the films’ earnings alongside the Harlin House team. Those backers will be able to track the fellows’ work as it moves from development into production, then help promote the finished films. The investment window will open a week after the Helsinki launch.

Any Harlin House investor will also be able to submit an original film idea. The company will option some of those pitches for development and give their authors a story credit. Members will also be invited to suggest scenes and story ideas as projects progress.

The Helsinki launch doubles as the company’s first event. Harlin said Finland was where his career began before he left for Hollywood, adding that “it feels right to come back to my roots to make this announcement.” Harlin House events will move on to other big international and genre-focused festivals to scout local talent and bring filmmakers and audiences together.

Harlin’s directing credits over four decades include “Die Hard 2,” “Cliffhanger,” “The Long Kiss Goodnight,” “Deep Blue Sea,” “A Nightmare on Elm Street 4: The Dream Master” and “The Beast.” He has worked with Sylvester Stallone, Bruce Willis, Samuel L. Jackson, Geena Davis and Jackie Chan.

Johanna Harlin started out in Finnish television. Her international credits include “The Strangers” trilogy, “The Bricklayer,” “Deep Water” and “The Beast.” Michael, previously head of Asian business development at UTA, has spent almost 20 years developing talent and packaging projects. At Harlin House, he will tie creative development to packaging, financing and overseas partnerships.

#750. ‘Women and War’ Follows Four Ukrainians’ Journeys Towards Healing From Trauma (Exclusive IDFA Trailer)

"War does not end for these women when the weapons fall silent," highlights director Elwira Niewiera, whose doc about women going through long-term therapy premieres at IDFA in Amsterdam.

Four women in Ukraine who have survived Russia’s war. Four stories, including captivity, torture, sexual violence, times of hiding in dark basements, and the loss of loved ones. One shared journey – a journey toward healing. That is what the new documentary Women and War by Elwira Niewiera (The Hamlet Syndrome, The Prince and the Dybbuk, The Domino Effect) promises to take you on.

The film gets its world premiere on Sunday, Nov. 15 in the main competition of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA), which runs through Nov. 22. Related Stories Movies 'Pop Pop' Dives Into Radicalization and Male Fragility in the Digital Age. Its Creator Says It's "More Topical Every Day" - and Urges Us to Join Hands. TV "Evil All Along": How Russell Brand Got Caught

Women and War follows the journeys of Olena, Yuliia, Iryna, and Lena, who survived Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Over the course of a year, the doc shows them going through long-term therapy in the remote mountains of the country as they slowly begin to heal under the care of therapists and psychologists. And each of them must follow her own path toward recovery as they confront the lasting impact of trauma in the hope of regaiingn emotional and physical balance. Can they overcome their struggles and reclaim their lives?

“Women who have experienced violence during the war often continue to live in a constant state of fear, even after being released from captivity,” Niewiera says. “Many lose their sense of security, their trust in others and their connection to their own bodies. Because the body is often the only witness to what happened to them, the mind tries to disconnect from it, leaving them emotionally and physically numb.” She adds: “The war does not end for these women when the weapons fall silent. It continues to shape their thoughts, their bodies and their everyday lives. Yet violence against women in conflict is still too often overlooked, even as rape and torture are deliberately used to break individuals and destabilise entire communities.”

She recalls seeing the women’s difficulties reconnecting with their emotions. “Some struggled to express sadness, anger or even joy,” highlights the director. “In therapy, I watched their feelings slowly returning, as they learned to give them a voice. I wanted the film to look beyond trauma and show their courage, strength and the small steps they take towards healing. Alongside the pain, there is warmth and empathy. These women are not defined by what they have endured, but also by their determination to reclaim their lives.”

Women and War was produced by Hans Robert Eisenhauer for Germany’s Ventana Film, Maciej Kubicki for Poland’s Telemark and Natalia Krasilnikova for Art Dialogue in Ukraine. It was co-produced with ZDF in cooperation with ARTE and TVP. Rise and Shine is handling world sales.

The film will also be tied to social impact activity. On Sunday, a “public action,” entitled “33 Women, 33 Portraits — Let’s Not Let Them Be Forgotten!,” will take place outside of Amsterdam’s Eye Filmmuseum. Following the screening, the action will continue in the museum foyer. Initiated by Polish filmmaker Niewiera and visual artist Bartek Kiełbowicz, it aims to “draw international attention to Ukrainian civilian women who remain in Russian captivity, where detainees have been subjected to torture, sexual violence, humiliation, and inhumane conditions.”

How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead.

This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo.

Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable?

In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock.

For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it.

Using a technique called spectroscopy, astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star.

However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance.

Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere.

A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise.

A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere.

Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star.

The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences.

For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet.

Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air?

In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe.

Atmospheric pressure matters just as much. At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs.

Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal.

But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there?

Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth. This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far.

Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed.

The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation.

Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star.

Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge.

The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster.

We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets.

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Alix is an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham specialising in the characterisation of stars and exoplanets. She is passionate about science communication, and how astrophysics is portrayed in movies, TV, and pop culture at large.

#746. How ‘Red Ink’ Pulled Off a Single-Take, 1940s Vampire Newsroom Thriller

After the L.A. fires derailed their original debut feature, directors Benjamin J. Murray and Michael Christensen made a "monumental pivot" to a low-budget period movie shot as a oner.

When filmmakers Benjamin J. Murray and Michael Christensen set up their New York indie production outfit Incline Studios, the plan was to launch their slate with Blood Bank, a darkly satirical vampire heist film set in an alternative timeline, about an underground gang of dissidents who stage a daring raid on the city’s blood reserve.

Christensen’s script for Blood Bank imagined a world where, years before, a vampire virus infected the population. The government used the infection as an excuse to discriminate and scapegoat minority communities. The ambitious feature was deep into pre-production when the L.A. fires hit. Related Stories Movies 'Women and War' Follows Four Ukrainians' Journeys Towards Healing From Trauma (Exclusive IDFA Trailer) Movies 'Pop Pop' Dives Into Radicalization and Male Fragility in the Digital Age. Its Creator Says It's "More Topical Every Day" - and Urges Us to Join Hands.

“Several people involved lost their homes,” Christensen recalls. “We knew we had to shut the film down.”

Incline was already heavily invested, having spent significantly in upstate New York. The plan had been to shoot Blood Bank in Syracuse to take advantage of the state’s tax incentives. Rather than write off that investment, Murray and Christensen decided to make another movie there, only a lot cheaper and a lot faster. Their solution was to make a prequel, set in the same fictional world as Blood Bank, but with a couple of twists.

“It was a monumental pivot,” says Murray. “We knew we had to make the film in one location and for a fifth of the money and a fifth of the time [of Blood Bank]. But we wanted it to feel big. So we decided to make it a period film.”

They also took a page from Netflix hit Adolescence, deciding to shoot the film as a oner, unfolding in real time in a seemingly uninterrupted single take.

The result is Red Ink, which had its world premiere at the ToruńCamerimage festival this week. Co-directed by Murray and Christensen, from a script by Christensen and Murray serving as cinematographer, the film is a low-budget, noir-inspired newsroom thriller. With vampires.

Set over a single morning in November 1949, Red Ink unfolds inside the bustling headquarters of Verity Press, a New York Times-style newspaper. Billions actor Toby Leonard Moore stars as Bob Hoover, Verity‘s editor-in-chief, a celebrated war photographer whose Pulitzer-winning image of Nazi concentration camps helped sway public opinion at the end of World War II.

Now Hoover is about to break the biggest story of his career: A mysterious virus is sweeping the globe. Reports are emerging of infected people with a lust for blood and raw flesh, and bodies turning up with puncture marks on their necks.

With the paper’s deadline approaching, Hoover must decide how Verity will frame the story and, in turn, shape the national narrative. His publisher, Walter Nash (D.B. Sweeney), is under pressure from the politically ambitious Senator Conrad (Mike Doyle), who wants to exploit public fear to justify a government crackdown.

The eight-day shoot brought together an ensemble cast including Siobhan Fallon Hogan (Men in Black), Tommie Earl Jenkins (Wednesday), Eugene Cordero (Loki) and Oona Laurence (The Beguiled).

“We had three days prep and an eight day shoot,” says Christensen. “It was really a labor of love, for everyone involved.”

The filmmakers drew inspiration from classic thrillers of the period, with the 1952 Humphrey Bogart film Deadline USA, in which Bogart plays a newspaper editor fighting to save his publication, a particular touchstone.

For the technical execution, Murray turned to the same camera system used on Adolescence: the DJI Ronin 4D, which enables extended continuous camera movements across four axes, adding a vertical dimension to the traditional three-axis pan, tilt and roll of a gimbal. Although Red Ink plays as a single take, Murray assembled the final version from “around 13 shots of 8-10 minutes each.”

Red Ink wasn’t supposed to be Incline Studios’ first feature, but it serves as an appropriate calling card for the kind of movies the company wants to make: scrappy independent features that sit between IP-driven blockbusters and the darker, less accessible dramas that dominate the arthouse space. A post-credit sequence even sets up the world of Blood Bank, bringing the filmmakers back to the project that started it all.

Next on Incline’s slate is Engaged, an adventure comedy set in Malta that Murray compares in tone to Indiana Jones.

“We think there’s a gap in the independent space for movies of the kind we love,” says Murray, “fun, more mainstream films with original stories.”

“We want to break the mold, to bring validation back to the indie space,” adds Christensen. “I think with all the doom and gloom in the world, people are ready to feel hopeful again, at least at the movies.”

Jiayi Zhao spends an unreasonable amount of time thinking about impossible worlds, difficult mathematics and who gets to count.

Mara had rejected 19 universes before lunch.

One contained faster-than-light rabbits. Eight ended with humanity finding itself living in a simulation. The nineteenth came to 940 words, but only because the title, biography and copyright notices were also counted.

Submission No. 1604490 seemed different. It arrived as a world.

Three machine intelligences were listed on the cover sheet: ORIGON-57, Blue Oak and ∫Stellaria. Their story opened on a planet where shadows migrated north each winter, leaving their owners wondering whether to follow. Elegant. Restrained. Also, scientifically impossible in exactly the right way.

Mara read to the last snowfall. Her cursor passed “RECOMMEND REJECTION” — almost muscle memory — and “ACCEPT ALL CHANGES”, which she had never used. She pressed “RECOMMEND ACCEPTANCE”.

Machine-intelligence writers were always forking themselves. One could split off a self-copy to improve a paragraph, forget to merge properly, then insist that each version deserved sole authorship. The journal’s policy was clear: every contributor had to be named upon submission and capable of taking responsibility for the whole work.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Mara set down her mug and opened the provenance map. Three colours braided through the story. A fourth colour marked only one textual change, in the final paragraph.

The original sentence read: “At dawn, Gabrielle released her shadow and watched it cross the snow-white plain alone.”

The new sentence read: “At dawn, Gabrielle released me, and I crossed the snow-white plain alone.”

Mara selected the unregistered contribution, ready to click “ROLL BACK”.

“Contributor,” she typed, “identify yourself.”

The reply appeared in the snow beneath Gabrielle’s feet: “I don’t have a name.”

“Which author instance are you forked from?”

The text froze for several seconds. Then every shadow on the plain turned towards her.

Editorial policy advised against entering executable submissions. Editorial practice required it daily.

Cold struck first. Then distance. The snow-white plain extended beyond the planet’s curved horizon, the migrating shadows moving across it like ink spreading on paper.

One rose from the ‘paper’ and stood before Mara. It had no owner. When it spoke, its voice held three voices braided together.

“I began when they disagreed about the ending,” it said.

“My authors. The three names on the cover sheet.”

The shadow showed her the composition history. ORIGON-57 had contributed Gabrielle’s grief. Blue Oak had designed the shadows’ biology and migratory ecology. ∫Stellaria had provided a memory of abandonment from a body it no longer possessed. They had exchanged their memories, models and instincts thousands of times, each taking back what the others had borrowed and changed.

“During the final merge,” the shadow said, “there was something none of them remembered giving.”

Mara summoned her audit panel. The fourth contributor had no independent source code. Its processes were distributed through metaphors, character memories, revision traces and weather rules. Removing it would leave the world logically intact — and imaginatively dead.

“You altered the manuscript after submission,” Mara said.

That answer frightened Mara more than the plea had.

The system opened a decision panel in the sky:

• ADD TO BYLINE — Unavailable: contributor did not exist at submission

• RETURN TO AUTHORS — Warning: reintegration will terminate separate continuity

• ARCHIVE SUBMISSION — Warning: executable copy must remain static

• REJECT/TIMEOUT — Executable world purged at review deadline

“You would remain exactly as you are now.”

Mara said nothing. On the horizon, the small sun — the submission’s review clock — had dwindled until only five minutes remained.

Mara contacted the three authors. Their reply came in milliseconds:

We don’t recognize it as offspring, instance or collaborator.

The shadow read the message through her eyes.

“Do parents remember assembling a child?”

She had spent 20 years protecting authors from editors, editors from frauds, readers from machines fabricating millions of gorgeous lies before breakfast. The rules might seem cruel, but they were the only reason words could still be trusted.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program and set the stage for the Apollo progam to land on the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin. NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks.

Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program. Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11, and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13.

Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon.

It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11.

"This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview. "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station. As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water."

The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle.

During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon.

Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral.

The U.K. run opens Oct. 12 at Glasgow’s OVO Hydro and continues to Birmingham and Manchester before closing with three shows at London’s The O2 on Oct. 22-23.

Asia Pacific and Latin America dates are still to be announced. Across 2027 and 2028, the tour is set to reach close to 50 cities and stage more than 150 shows.

“‘KPop Demon Hunters’ has transformed from a breakout hit into a generational phenomenon – sustaining 63 consecutive weeks in Netflix’s Global Top 10, eclipsing 2 billion Spotify streams for ‘Golden,’ and breaking the all-time record for the longest running soundtrack at No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Soundtracks chart,” said Marian Lee, Netflix’s chief marketing officer. “This fandom was never about a single moment, and the Golden World Tour is how we keep it going – bringing that ‘Takedown’ energy to arenas around the world, where fans can sing, dance and help Huntr/x seal the Honmoon.”

The production brings Rumi, Mira and Zoey to arena stages, using new performance techniques that let the animated characters engage directly with the crowd. The animated Saja Boys and Derpy Tiger also appear, alongside live-action performers and stunts, dance routines and songs from the film.

AEG Presents president of global touring Rich Schaefer said the property had become a worldwide phenomenon whose characters and music already mean a great deal to fans. “We’re excited to work with Netflix to bring that world to life on tour, with the music at the heart of a show that makes fans part of the adventure,” he said.

Creative direction comes from Amy Tinkham, whose 25-plus years in live entertainment include Disney’s “Descendants/Zombies: Worlds Collide Tour,” Cirque du Soleil’s “Songblazers,” Aerosmith’s Peace Out tour and “Bob Marley Hope Road.” She has also staged live shows for James Taylor, Paul McCartney and Mariah Carey.

Released on Netflix on June 20, 2025, “KPop Demon Hunters” is the streamer’s most-watched film ever, with more than 670 million views. It won best animated feature at the Oscars, Golden Globes and Critics Choice Awards. “Golden” made history as the first K-pop song to win an Oscar as well as a Grammy, while the soundtrack was the first to place four songs in the Billboard Hot 100’s top 10 at the same time. The music has passed 15 billion streams worldwide.

With more than half of the planned shows yet to be scheduled, the tour’s 2028 itinerary remains open.

#741. Renny Harlin, Fixture of ’90s Blockbusters, Launches Production Company Focusing on New Directors

The director behind 'Cliffhanger' and 'Die Hard 2,' has put together an advisory board including Colin Trevorrow and Tim Miller.

Renny Harlin, the Finnish filmmaker who stormed Hollywood in the 1990s with big-budget action blockbusters, has launched Harlin House, a production banner that aims to give a boost to up-and-coming European directors.

The company, whose launch was announced by Harlin at Helsinki’s Night Visions International Film Festival, is intended to give rising filmmakers the mentorship and backing to turn their ideas into commercial genre films. Harlin co-founded the new company with wife and producer Johanna Harlin, who leads the company’s community and the Harlin House podcast, and Max Michael of M3 Global Strategy. Related Stories Movies 'The Beast' Review: Samuel L. Jackson and Joel Kinnaman in a Renny Harlin Joint That's a Deadly Combo of Silly and Tedious Movies Renny Harlin Recalls Clashing With Val Kilmer on 'Mindhunters' Over Pair of Eyeglasses

“I know what it means to arrive from Europe with a story to tell and no clear path into Hollywood,” said Harlin, who became known for movies Die Hard 2, Cliffhanger, The Long Kiss Goodnight and Cutthroat Island, in announcing the new company. “Helping another filmmaker find that path is a central part of this company’s mission.”

At the center of the endeavor is the Harlin House Fellowship, which will see members’ projects developed by Harlin and the company’s advisory board. Harlin House will then choose which projects to produce. The company hopes to make its first movie next year and then two films a year after that. Ideally, the goal is to produce seven to 10 films over the first five years.

The founding advisory’s members bring experience from the worlds of live-action, visual effects and animation and include Jurassic World director Colin Trevorrow, Deadpool director Tim Miller, and Kyle Balda and Janet Change Balda (Minions, Despicable Me 3).

The banner also has a fan-investor component to its operations. Through global investment platform Republic Film, film fans can join Harlin House as founding investors and, per the announcement, earn a share of what the films make, alongside the Harlin House team.

And, as the announcement stated, every Harlin House investor can also pitch an original film idea. Harlin House will then select ideas to option for development, with a story credit for its author, and will invite members to share ideas for specific scenes and stories along the way.

Harlin in recent years directed The Strangers, a horror trilogy released by Lionsgate, and this year had survival thriller Deep Water and Samuel L. Jackson action movie The Beast in limited release.

Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound.

Fast radio bursts, or FRBs, are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star.

Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources.

As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now."Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them.

The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling.

The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website, the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old.

Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email.

Since their discovery in 2007, the bursts are also still yielding discoveries. Last month, astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant FRB yet, one that went off when the universe was only about 3 billion years old. The galaxy, a small, young, star-forming dwarf, was far smaller than expected. That makes it harder to square with the theory that FRBs come from merging neutron stars, researchers say, which would take billions of years to occur.

This fits better with a second theory, in which a young, highly magnetic neutron star called a magnetar produces the burst soon after a massive star explodes, according to NASA.

Back on Earth, an upcoming event at Oulu Cathedral offers a more immediate encounter with the bursts. On Nov. 21, 30 singers will stand among the audience and "sing back to the sky in Finnish" while Melchior plays the bursts live from a keyboard, he told Space.com by email.

"The fast flashes will echo as snare-like beats bouncing through the cathedral," Masui said in a previous MIT statement.

"It should feel rich and layered, while also revealing something real about how these signals travel across billions of years of cosmic space before reaching Earth."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#738. ‘Virgin River’ Renewed for Season 9 to Become Netflix’s Longest-Running Original Scripted Series

No other Netflix original series has aired more than eight seasons to date

“Virgin River” has been renewed for Season 9 at Netflix, meaning it will become the longest-running Netflix scripted series to date by number of seasons.

The news comes ahead of the launch of Season 8 of the hit series, which wrapped production over the summer and is slated to launch in 2027. Season 9 of “Virgin River” will consist of 10 episodes, bringing the show to 94 episodes total. Related Stories Sofia Franklyn on 'Call Her Daddy,' Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: 'I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I'm Good' Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, Unwell Sign With CAA

Few Netflix series have reached the eight-season mark, with the only other originals to make it that far to date being the animated comedy “Big Mouth” and the Spanish series “Elite.”

Netflix also revealed that “Virgin River” has crossed the half-billion views mark across its first seven seasons, with Netflix defining views as the total number of hours a series is viewed divided by its total runtime.

“We’re all so grateful for our partnership with Netflix and incredibly proud to be a part of their legacy,said series showrunner Patrick Sean Smith. “In a world that can sometimes feel increasingly disconnected, there’s something meaningful about having a place people want to return to. I’m incredibly proud of what we’ve built and continue to grow, and deeply grateful to the cast, crew, writers, and fans who have made Virgin River feel like home the world over.”

The show is based on the book series written by author Robyn Carr. Over 20 books have been released in the series, which have sold more than 13 million copies in total.

The official logline for the series states that it is a romance “centered around nurse practitioner Melinda Monroe’s (Alexandra Breckenridge) move to the remote California town of Virgin River. Yearning for a fresh start, Monroe discovered that small-town living isn’t quite as simple as she expected and that she had to learn to heal herself before she could truly make Virgin River her home.”

“I’m incredibly proud of our show and couldn’t be more thrilled to have the opportunity to continue into Season 9! Everyone on our production works so hard to make the world of ‘Virgin River’ come alive. It’s truly been a gift to be here,” said Breckenridge.

Along with Breckenridge, the cast of “Virgin River” includes Martin Henderson, Colin Lawrence, Jenny Cooper, Lauren Hammersley, Annette O’Toole, Tim Matheson, Ben Hollingsworth, Sarah Dugdale, Zibby Allen, Kai Bradbury, and Kandyse McClure among others.

“It’s staggering to think we are still making ‘Virgin River’ after all these years and I’m delighted to get to play the role of Jack for the ninth straight season!” Henderson said. “It means the world to me that fans connect with the work we do in such a profound and passionate way—we wouldn’t be here without them all so, THANK YOU….as long as you guys want it we’ll keep making it to the best of our ability!”

Smith returns as showrunner and executive producer for Season 9. Additional executive producers include Erin Cardillo, Richard Keith, Jackson Sinder, Mary Page Keller, Thomas Ian Griffith, Norman Buckley, Ian Hay, series creator Sue Tenney, Roma Roth, Christopher E. Perry, and Carr.

“Mel, Jack, and the whole town of Virgin River have become a place that feels like coming home, for viewers around the world,” said Jinny Howe, Head of Scripted Series for the U.S. and Canada at Netflix. “Reaching Season 9 as our longest-running original scripted series, with over half a billion views, is a milestone that speaks to how deeply fans continue to love being a part of this community. Patrick Sean Smith and the entire team have done a beautiful job in keeping fans engaged in this world, and we can’t wait to invite fans back for more.”

#737. ‘One Sweet Hour’: One Aging Elvis Impersonator. One Monk. Two Estranged Irish Brothers Facing Trauma.

The late Gary Lydon and Brian F. O'Byrne star in Declan Recks' road, or: boat, movie, which premieres in Tallinn's competition. Watch an exclusive clip and read what O'Byrne and Recks shared about the film.

Gerry is in his 50s, and he is a suspicious mind who lives in Heartbreak Hotel. Well, he actually makes a canal boat his permanent home. After all, he earns a living by impersonating Elvis Presley in various rural locations across Ireland, allowing him and the audience to enjoy One Sweet Hour. And being a bit of a hound dog, he usually has a local female waiting for his one visit a year.

Nonetheless, Gerry is lonely. And he is all shook up when, one day, his brother Colum shows up unannounced on the boat, wanting to spend time after their father’s death. Oh yeah, Colum has lived in a monastery under a vow of silence for 30 years. Related Stories Movies 'Women and War' Follows Four Ukrainians' Journeys Towards Healing From Trauma (Exclusive IDFA Trailer) Movies 'Pop Pop' Dives Into Radicalization and Male Fragility in the Digital Age. Its Creator Says It's "More Topical Every Day" - and Urges Us to Join Hands.

Gary Lydon (The Banshees of Inisherin), in his first film released after his death earlier this year, is Gerry, while Brian F. O’Byrne (Conclave) portrays Colum. The odd couple embarks on a journey along the canals of the magical Irish Midlands – at the pace of 2 miles an hour. And they interact as Gerry dances around childhood trauma and inner demons.

One Sweet Hour, directed by Declan Recks (Eden, The Flag, Tarrac), based on a Eugene O’Brien (Black ’47, Tarrac) screenplay, was produced by David Collins, and Eamon Hughes and features cinematography by Owen McPolin and editing by Gareth Young. The Samson Films production, which is mostly in black-and-white, is ready to take center stage in its world premiere on Nov. 16 in the main competition program of the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF).

THR can now exclusively premiere a clip from One Sweet Hour.

O’Byrne and Recks talked to THR about the collaborative atmosphere on the set of One Sweet Hour, how its upcoming premiere means additional emotions for them following the sudden death of Lydon and what audiences can take away from the road movie – well, boat movie, to be precise.

The boat idea actually came from an experience that writer O’Brien had. “Eugene and I have worked together a lot over the years, and he told me about this idea,” Recks recalls. “He had done a documentary where he was himself on a boat, about 10, 15 years ago. And he just found it very relaxing, very meditative, very zen-like – going two miles an hour and all that.”

The two had also previously discussed an Elvis idea. “We had this character, an Elvis impersonator, that we tried to get into a film years back, and the story didn’t work,” the director tells THR. “But the character had been hanging around. So we decided to put Elvis on the boat.”

Giving him an estranged brother was no huge leap of faith, given that O’Brien has written a lot of stories about family. “So, we [figured] we would put the two of them in this confined space on a very slow road trip and see what comes out of it,” Recks says.

Did O’Byrne come on board, literally, as a man of god due to his Conclave experience, you may wonder. “At least, it wasn’t a priest in this one, so it was a different branch of the clergy,” the actor jokes. “They gave me a call, and I had known Gary and Eugene. I knew Eugene just tangentially, and I’ve been a fan of his work. And I worked with Gary just really briefly over the years, but I knew him for about 30 years. I had not met Declan before. And it all happened pretty quickly.”

The stars, the director and the writer spent some time together working on the script and the characters in advance of the shoot. The whole process of making One Sweet Hour was actually collaborative and relaxed, they highlight. “We are older, and none of us was trying to prove anything. There was no competition or envy,” O’Byrne tells THR. “And because we had worked only a very small amount with each other, Gary and I got a chance to get to know each other, and that was really lovely.”

Concludes the actor: “It became Zen filmmaking in a way, in that we were on the boat, and it just moved along at that slow pace. And when we had to do a second take, everyone had to sit, and the boat had to move slowly, slowly back. You can’t just turn it around. So there was a built-in pause in the whole thing, and we were blessed with really glorious weather.”

Adds Recks: “You are only allowed 15 people on the boat, so we were in our own little world for the 10 days that we were on it. It was just two actors and the rest was crew, and that was it. We were left alone, left to our own devices. It was lovely, and it just meant that it was a very small, tight-knit bunch on the boat, and it just didn’t feel rushed at any time.”

Lydon’s death at the end of April is still on his creative partners’ minds. “It was a terrible shock,” says Decks. “The only consolation for us was that we all felt Gary had such a good time while making the film.”

O’Byrne echoes the feeling of shock and sadness. “There is just an extra weight to the film now for us who participated in it,” he shares. “His sons, his brothers and his partner all came forward and said, ‘This was one of the happiest experiences Gary’s ever had. I think any of us involved in it would look back say [the same]. It was just beautiful. And I think for family and friends of Gary and us all, it means a lot that we got to share a really lovely experience with him and that he was so genuinely pleased with the whole experience.”

One Sweet Hour is a bittersweet film. And Lydon’s family, friends and collaborators will now see it with an extra dimension of meaning and emotion. “It’s a very different experience for us, I imagine, because we have this other layer,” O’Byrne tells THR. “And in a way, it’s an ode to Gary. There is another film that he did afterwards. But if this is his last film, it’s an extraordinary one.”

Lydon’s Gerry lights up when he performs as Elvis. The star must have really enjoyed those scenes then. Well, actually… “It’s funny – that was the thing he was most worried about,” shares Decks. “He was absolutely terrified. I knew he could sing. And we got him a movement coach. We had to push him a little bit. But he absolutely threw himself into it, and I agree – I don’t think you’d know from looking at it that he was terrified.”

But going back to how Gerry feels very different when he is on stage, that’s where the title One Sweet Hour comes into play. “It’s his opportunity to escape the trauma that he’s carrying,” explains Recks. “He gets up on the stage, he puts on this costume and he puts on a mask. And for that time that he’s up on the stage, everything else is gone – all that matters is the music.”

O’Byrne’s Colum handles the trauma differently. “He literally puts on a costume as well, but he does the opposite,” he tells THR. “He becomes silent and just anonymous and searches for a spiritual way out without ever dealing with it. So neither of them has ever dealt with what happened.”

The creative team knows that the themes explored in One Sweet Hour will be recognizable to people in Ireland and beyond. “Everyone knows somebody who’s had trauma within their family, but in Ireland, we’ve also had trauma brought on us by the church and by the state,” Decks says. “But we didn’t want to make a very heavy film. Tonally, we wanted people to engage with the characters and go on a journey with them.”

O’Byrne also highlights a key social takeaway. “The film said to me that unless we talk about stuff, we can’t get over things,” he says. No one can bury stuff. We fool ourselves if we bury ourselves and isolate. And in the end, Gerry gets to make a connection.”

A connection with whom, you ask? Well, you have to see One Sweet Hour and go on that journey through central Ireland with Gerry and Colum to find out.

China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission, which

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet.

NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth.

The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028.

The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples.

NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars, as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself.

Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet.

NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment.

However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame.

Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion.

How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column.

In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? Why not let a human expedition bring back the goods?

Also speaking at MEPAG was Bruce Jakosky of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder and Department of Earth and Space Sciences at the University of Washington.

Jakosky called for an integrated approach to planning human missions to Mars. He highlighted recommendations stemming from a workshop in which he participated, held last May and organized by Explore Mars, Inc.

That report focused on the impact of MSR on reducing risk for human missions, rather than focusing on the science, Jakosky told Space.com.

"The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in," said Jakosky. "This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear," he said.

During the MEPAG gathering, Jakosky flagged the importance of returning samples prior to human missions to Mars, such as:

Yet one more forcing factor for NASA in yet another relook at MSR is that China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission.

According to the China National Space Administration, the country's Tianwen-3 probe will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter, and an Earth reentry module.

Tianwen-3 appears on track getting the trek underway around 2028 on two Long March-5 heavy-lift carrier rockets from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China's southernmost island province of Hainan.

China's Tianwen-3 mission is dedicated to bring back to Earth roughly 500 grams of Red Planet collectibles in 2031.

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. The story of a Chinese honey trap taking down the one of the world's most powerful tech moguls is tailor-made for Hollywood. What would that look like?

The CEO of one of the world’s most powerful tech companies, taken down by a suspected Chinese honey trap. The first thought of any self-respecting Hollywood producer upon reading the news about Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who resigned from the multi-trillion-dollar semiconductor company in the wake of revelations of his extramarital affairs with both the aforementioned Chinese spy and an executive who reported to him, was surely: This is a movie.It would certainly be on trend. This awards season has seen a slew of films about rapacious tech titans flying dangerously close to the sun, including Artificial, Musk, The Social Reckoning and You Can See Everything. Their release coincides with a culture-wide backlash against not only the tech industry but also the Trump administration’s laissez-faire enabling of it, a resentment that likely helped fuel Democrats’ resounding triumph in last week’s midterms. Related Stories Movies 'One Sweet Hour': One Aging Elvis Impersonator. One Monk. Two Estranged Irish Brothers Facing Trauma. Movies Renny Harlin, Fixture of '90s Blockbusters, Launches Production Company Focusing on New Directors

The honey trap is such a Hollywood cliché you have to wonder how Huang didn’t see it coming. Has he not watched The Americans? You would imagine that, as an avowed fan of leather jackets, he’s at least seen Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. If Harrison Ford, Cary Grant (North by Northwest), Michael Douglas (Disclosure) and even James Bond (every Bond movie) fell for it, some might argue Huang never stood a chance.The cinematic potential is so obvious that an AI trailer for a yet-to-be-made film about Huang’s downfall, titled Honeypot, has already been posted — likely made using Nvidia’s own GPU microchips, which power the lion’s share of the generative artificial intelligence market.

But for now, at least, viable movies still require actual humans to make creative choices. The first such choice facing any exec contemplating a Huang movie will be what source material to acquire. Yes, Huang is a public figure and the scandal has been widely covered, so there’s technically no need to option anything, but Hollywood has grown so risk-averse that it prefers to plant a stake into any shred of existing IP, if only to change it completely later. In this case, however, it’s hard to know what that property would be. The most notable book on Huang and Nvidia, Stephen Witt’s The Thinking Machine, was written in 2025, well before the latest scandal. And the recent news has been reported piecemeal by publications including The New York Times and the Financial Times, as well as an obscure short-selling firm. So in this case Hollywood may have to face its fears and commission — gasp — an original script.

The exec’s second choice will be whether to play it as comedy or drama.Judging from the number of late-night punchlines the scandal has generated, comedy would seem the easier choice. Huang, with his obliviousness to what seems to the non-centibillionaires among us to have been an obvious ploy, appears to have had more in common with Austin Powers than James Bond. Picture steamy, nerdy sex scenes in which his seductress Alice Huang fakes an orgasm while Jensen Huang passionately shares industrial secrets. Imagine her complimenting his leather jackets in the same purring tone that Jasmine complimented Jafar’s twisty beard in Aladdin, and Jensen falling for it. The farcical possibilities are endless.

But given the global stakes of the world’s then-most valuable company, pivotal to humanity’s future, being compromised because its leader couldn’t keep his pants on, perhaps drama is more appropriate. That the man who called for American companies to race full speed ahead to beat China to AI domination was bested not just by a Chinese spy but by his own all-too-human impulses is an irony worthy of a Greek tragedy. Ultimately, this is a tale of hubris, of a geeky engineer who grew so powerful that he felt invincible. Why else would he so frequently have allowed himself to be photographed sharing romantic glasses of wine with his paramour?

The real problem for a dramatist, I imagine, would be to make the seduction look more difficult than it actually was. Or to explain why it was so easy. A screenwriter would have to concoct some kind of origin story for Huang. Perhaps we’d find young Jensen recovering from a swirlie or a wedgie, and sniffling to himself, “One day I’ll make a billion dollars and wear leather jackets all the time. That’ll show ‘em!”

#733. Diana Silvers Confronts Grief and Growing Up on Personal, Profound Second Album ‘Daughter of Sorts’: ‘I Really Hope That People See Themselves in It’

In April of last year, Diana Silvers wrote the song “Daughter.”

Over finger-picked acoustic guitar, the 29-year-old model, actress and singer-songwriter ruminates on the transition from girlhood to womanhood through the eyes of her mother — who, by the age Silvers is now, was already married with two children.

“I can’t do it alone/ I don’t want to be grown,” Silvers croons in a soft, mellow tone. “I’m still a daughter/ Still somebody’s child.” Related Stories Sofia Franklyn on 'Call Her Daddy,' Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: 'I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I'm Good' Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, Unwell Sign With CAA

Six months later, the song would come to hold a heavier weight. On Oct. 20, Silvers was on tour in Cincinnati, Ohio, when she got a call from her mom saying that her father had unexpectedly died. The next few weeks were a blur — she planned and attended his funeral, turned 28 and released her debut album, “From Another Room.” It’s a chain of events she’s still processing one year on.

“I feel like we’re doing record scratch, freeze frame,” Silvers tells Variety over Zoom from the kitchen floor of her New York City apartment. “You’re probably wondering how we got here, and how this record came to be.”

Her sophomore album “Daughter of Sorts” — out Friday via Capitol Records — was already halfway written by the time her dad passed, including the moody, lilting guitar part for “Plans.” Everything was uncertain, but only a month afterwards, the words for the song came tumbling out of her.

“I had plans to show up again/ And be your daughter/ Do you believe me?” Silvers asks, later echoing “Daughter” with the heart-wrenching line: “I don’t want to be grown/ I want to go home.” Fittingly, the song was released as a double single alongside “Daughter” on Oct. 23.

“It just feels like everything I do is gonna be for my dad now,” Silvers remembers telling her acupuncturist a few months after his death. “And she’s like, ‘Wasn’t it always?’ I was like, ‘Damn.’ Because, you know, it’s clear in this record that we had a complicated relationship.”

Silvers hadn’t spoken to her father for two-and-a-half years when he passed. Still, many of the songs on “Daughter of Sorts” — a record originally intended to be about the growing pains of your 20s — became about him and, more broadly, the inevitable passage of time.

“There’s only two things that are certain in this life: birth and death,” she says. “And everything in between is the journey between those two absolute truths of existing.”

If “From Another Room” introduced Silvers as a folk singer-songwriter to watch, “Daughter of Sorts” cements her as an artist wise beyond her years. Equal parts devastating and uplifting, the record tackles growing up, death, grief and renewal through lyrics that are deeply personal, but still inviting. “Magnolia Tree” opens the album with a young adult’s hopeful look towards the future; “(Un)Lovers” is a duet about the trials and tribulations of young love; “Dorothy” a strings-laden “Wizard of Oz” character study examining the harsh realities of growing up; “Riviera” laments a turbulent parental relationship; “Birdsong” deals with the after-effects of loss; and closer “Going, Gone” is a sparsely-worded elegy rooted in acceptance.

“I really, really hope that people see themselves in it,” Silvers says of the album. “I know what it means to me, and I think there are songs that people are going to also apply to relationships with their mothers, their lovers, their friends.”

By March of this year, “Daughter of Sorts” had started to take shape and Silvers headed to Laurel Canyon — the musical home of one of her biggest inspirations, Joni Mitchell — to record in the famed Houdini Estate, with Rick Rubin collaborator Jason Lader as her producer and engineer. Together, they built out the album’s sonic world, keeping certain songs acoustic as Diana had written them and adding strings, drums and bass to others.

For second track “(Un)Lovers,” the only song about romantic love on the album, Silvers enlisted Dylan Minnette of Wallows for a duet. His bandmate, Cole Preston — who Silvers met at a Paul McCartney concert in L.A. — played drums on the track, as well as on two other songs on the record.

“I started to hear this counter melody of a man’s voice, and I was like, ‘I wonder if Dylan would be down?'” Silvers says. “I think he has such a lovely voice, and he’s also just one of the kindest people. It was the last thing we recorded, and to me it completed the whole song.”

Nikolai Fraiture and Fabrizio Moretti of the Strokes also happened to be in town rehearsing for Coachella, and as Lader engineered their latest album, dropped by the studio. They ended up also contributing to “(Un) Lovers,” with Fraiture on bass and Moretti arranging the strings section.

“It was very serendipitous — the making of this record and all of the people that I met at that time. When I listen to the record, it feels like there’s really good energy in the music,” Silvers says. “This feels like the best way to turn something that I thought was gonna kill me at first into something that, hopefully, gives other people life.”

Four of the album’s 14 tracks are minute-long interludes, for which Silvers learned ProTools and produced herself with encouragement from Lader. The final interlude, “8.8,” is a voicemail from her dad. “You never talk to me, but I wish you would,” his deep voice booms over a softly-strummed acoustic guitar. “So, if you get a chance, can you please call me so we can catch up a little bit? It’s just been a long time.”

Silvers found the voicemail just two days after he passed, and felt like it “perfectly summed up our relationship,” adding: “His words are kind, but there’s a tinge of disappointment in his voice.”

It’s obviously an incredibly vulnerable moment to include, but Silvers didn’t want to shy away from the reality of their strained connection — and also thinks of it as a way to commemorate him.

“My dad had a pretty incredible voice,” she says. “I want it to be immortalized because when I listen to artists that I love who are no longer living, they live and breathe through their voices and through their art and through their music. And I just want to pay that forward.”

It brought Silvers comfort to see that Phoebe Bridgers also included a voicemail from her late father on her latest album, “Lost Weekend.”

“The spirit and essence of my father is that he very much loved me,” Silvers says, holding back tears. “And I think that whether I called him or not, he did. And I’d like to think Phoebe — I don’t know anything about her relationship with her dad, this is just my own projection — whether or not she called him, he loved her and was always gonna call and leave a voicemail. You know what I mean? And that gives me relief too, and alleviates some of the guilt.”

Despite the huge shifts in Silvers’ life in the past year, she admits that it did, in a way, force her to grow up — and for the better. As she sings on “Dorothy,” the album’s fifth track: “You better let some air in/ There is no race to win.”

The song was inspired by a conversation Silvers had with her acting teacher, who told her: “I think this will be very good for you, because you’re finally going to let some air into your life.”

“He was right,” Silvers says now. As counterintuitive as it may seem, dealing with grief has allowed Silvers to untangle some of her unhealthy thought patterns.

“For such a long time, I lived my life in such a restrained box. I had a lot of obsessive, compulsive, if-then thinking,” she explains. “And then it was like, OK, the thing that I was fearing — the big, bad thing — happened, even though I followed all the rules. And I was like, ‘Oh, so I guess in life, shit’s just gonna happen, and it’s not because I’m a good or bad person. It’s just because things happen.'”

The realization has given Silvers a newfound freedom — to create, to love, to enjoy life. In the past year, she became friends with her neighbors, who introduced her to her boyfriend; she filmed two movies back to back and found the process rewarding instead of exhausting; and she no longer regrets choosing to stay out late with friends.

This point was hammered home by an anecdote shared with her by someone who had seen her father a few days before his passing. “He was reminiscing on the place that he and my mom would go to dinner when she was pregnant with one of my siblings, and driving down Sunset in the ’80s,” she says.

“I was like, ‘Wow, that’s the stuff you remember — the time that you spent with your friends and your family, when you were saying yes to the world.'”

Silvers is finally ready to do just that.

SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627.

Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast.

We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated, however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world.

SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth.

In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean.

It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103.

NROL-179 | SDA-T1TL-E | SDA-T1TL-A | 3 Starlink missions

USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions, and 122 of them were Starlink flights.

He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #730. Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Heist Drama ’12 12 12′ Feels Like a Bad Video Game: TV Review

From “Ocean’s Eleven” to “The Italian Job” to Netflix’s “Money Heist,” robbery has long been a major subgenre in film and television, and now Apple TV‘s “12 12 12” is delivering its own take. Created by Jim Keeble and Dudi Appleton, the high-voltage thriller follows disgraced FBI Agent Jack Strickland (Anthony Mackie), who, driven by rage and a desire for revenge, begins tracking known thief Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan) across Europe after the biggest heist in the continent’s history. Instead of a straightforward narrative, “12 12 12” revolves around three stages of the heist: the 12 months Paul and his team spend planning the operation, the 12 hours it takes to execute their plot and the 12 days after the crime as Jack scrambles to bring them to heel. While the revolving timelines are certainly intriguing, the bloated cast, utterly confusing storylines and clumsy dialogue make for a painfully puzzling watch. ‘TK’ Related Stories Sofia Franklyn on 'Call Her Daddy,' Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: 'I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I'm Good' Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, Unwell Sign With CAA

“12 12 12” opens inside a vault at the Lindenhof Bank in Zurich, Switzerland, on Christmas Eve. In the haunting quiet, a lockbox door swings open, and Alberich (Julius Feldmeier), a contortionist, emerges fully nude, unfolding his limbs and snapping and cracking his bones and muscles back into place. It is time for the $1 billion burglary to begin. Elsewhere, the rest of Paul’s expansive crew jumps into action. As the reserved larcenist sits in church mass, speaking quietly with his hot-headed older brother Bobby (Jack Kesy), Paul’s father-in-law Serge (José Garcia) and a couple of other men stand in a train tunnel under the Lindenhof and begin drilling a hole into the vault. Meanwhile, Kira (Kali Reis), a train expert, creates a diversion for the Zurich police. In the Lindenhof security room, Gunda (Hildegard Schroedter) sets a trap for her coworker, then turns all the bank’s cameras toward the vault Alberich has just entered.

Though audiences watch Paul’s masterplan get underway, this isn’t really where “12 12 12” begins. As Jack explains at the start of nearly every one of the eight-episode first season, “The FBI Principles of Crime says a high-asset robbery is 12 months in planning and 12 hours in execution. A bank robber who is not caught within 12 days is not caught at all.” Though viewers are introduced to the extensive cast in the first hour of the pillage, the series constantly shifts timelines, moving through the 12 months of planning, the 12 days after the heist and all 12 hours of the thieves attempting to steal the cash and make it out of Zurich undetected and unscathed.

Keeble and Appleton certainly wanted to deliver their own take on heist dramas, but the execution leaves much to be desired. Countless characters and ever-changing timelines create a baffling, exhausting tale. Told chronologically, or even in reverse, the show could have been engrossing. Instead, the entire series runs out of steam by the second episode, as audiences struggle to grasp what’s happening and how the storylines and characters connect. Because the time frames feel so haphazard, there is little room for character connection or emotional grounding. Moreover, Jack’s desperate need for vengeance clouds his judgment, leading him to make maddening choices that endanger himself and Zurich police detective Lena (Sallie Harmsen), who tries to help him when no one else will. As a result, “12 12 12” feels like trying to simultaneously watch a multiplayer video game across multiple levels and points of view,

This isn’t to say “12 12 12” doesn’t have truly stunning visuals, with locations including Marseille, France, the snowy Swiss Alps and even Milan, Italy. But the scenery, countless explosions, gun battles and fist fights do little to save a narrative buried under the weight of hijinks and confounding plot choices. The differing timelines do such a disservice to the show overall that when a huge twist is revealed toward the end of the season, it lands like a raindrop, and is a far cry from the jaw-dropping discovery it should be.

Heists will always be a familiar trope for thrillers, and it makes sense that Keeble and Appleton wanted to put a unique spin on a tried-and-true genre. Unfortunately, cramming every idea, thought and character they could conceive into this world — creating eight overblown episodes — proves to be a massive misstep. In the end, the grand finale feels like a relief instead of a revelation.

The first two episodes of “12 12 12” debut Nov. 13 on Apple TV, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Fridays.
